blocks.h: (a) Requirements for classification, and the role of the society — 8 marks
1. What classification is, and the line between class and statutory work

blocks.p: Classification is a private, contractual certification of technical fitness against a society's own published rules. A classification society develops rules for the structure, machinery and electrical installations of a ship, approves the design against them, surveys the ship during construction and then surveys her periodically in service. If she complies, the society assigns and maintains class and issues a Certificate of Class.
Two consequences follow immediately, and a Class I answer states both.

ul: Class is not law. It is a contract between the owner and the society. The society's remedy for non-compliance is to impose a condition, suspend or withdraw class — not to detain the ship.

Class is nevertheless commercially compulsory. Hull and machinery underwriters, P&I clubs, charterers, financiers and flag Administrations all require it, so a ship out of class is effectively unemployable and uninsurable. Withdrawal of class is the sharpest sanction in the industry precisely because it is not a legal one.

blocks.p: The statutory work — SOLAS, MARPOL, Load Line, Tonnage, ISM, ISPS, MLC — belongs to the flag Administration. It only reaches a classification society because the Administration delegates it. Keeping those two ideas apart is what limb (b) then tests.

blocks.h: 2. The requirements a ship must satisfy to be assigned class

blocks.p: Classification is not a single event. It is a sequence of requirements running from the drawing board to the end of the ship's life, and the marks in this limb are in that sequence.

ol: Application and rule selection. The owner applies to the society; the applicable rule set is fixed by ship type, size, service and intended notations — and for bulk carriers and oil tankers by the IACS Common Structural Rules.

Plan approval. Structural drawings, midship section, scantlings, shafting and propeller, main and auxiliary machinery, piping, electrical single-line diagrams and control systems are submitted and approved against the rules before construction.

Approval and certification of materials and components. Steel, castings, forgings, welding consumables, main engine, boilers, pressure vessels, shafting, anchors and chain cables are made at approved works under survey and issued with certificates.

Survey during construction. The society's surveyor attends the yard to verify that the ship is being built to the approved plans — alignment, welding and NDT, tank testing, sea trials and machinery trials.

Assignment of class. On satisfactory completion the society assigns a class notation and issues the Certificate of Class. The notations record the basis on which she was built — hull and machinery character marks, service restriction, ice class, UMS, and any special notation.

Maintenance of class in service. Class is retained only by a continuing survey regime: annual, intermediate and five-yearly renewal surveys, docking or in-water surveys, tailshaft and boiler surveys, and machinery surveyed either at renewal or on a rolling continuous-survey or approved planned-maintenance basis.

Reporting of damage and of change. The owner must report damage, grounding, defects and repairs affecting class, and must not alter classed items without approval. Failure to do so is itself a breach.

Conditions of Class. Where a defect impairs compliance, the surveyor imposes a time-bound requirement to rectify. Class continues meanwhile; if the condition is not cleared by its due date, class is suspended.

blocks.p: All of that is class practice and the IACS framework. It is not a SOLAS requirement, and stating it as one is the commonest error in this question.

blocks.h: 3. Where class rules acquire legal force, and how the society ensures compliance

blocks.p: The society becomes legally relevant at two distinct points, and they are different mechanisms.

First, SOLAS adopts class rules as the construction standard. Regulation II-1/3-1 provides that, in addition to the requirements elsewhere in the regulations, ships shall be designed, constructed and maintained in compliance with the structural, mechanical and electrical requirements of a classification society which is recognized by the Administration in accordance with regulation XI-1/1, or with applicable national standards of the Administration which provide an equivalent level of safety. That single regulation is what converts a private rulebook into the operative construction standard for a Convention ship — and note the words designed, constructed AND MAINTAINED, which is why the survey cycle, not just the newbuilding survey, is a SOLAS matter.

Second, the Administration may delegate the statutory work itself. Regulation I/6 places inspection and survey on officers of the Administration, but permits the Administration to entrust them to nominated surveyors or to recognized organizations. Regulation XI-1/1 then requires that authorisation to be given in accordance with the RO Code (resolution MSC.349(92)), whose parts 1 and 2 are mandatory and part 3 recommendatory. The RO Code sets what an organisation must be and must do to be recognised, and how the Administration must oversee it.

So the society ensures compliance in two capacities that must never be confused: as classification society, enforcing its own rules by conditions of class and ultimately withdrawal; and as Recognized Organization, acting for the flag State under a specific delegation, issuing statutory certificates in the Administration's name. Under regulation I/6 the RO must at minimum be empowered to require repairs and to survey at a port State's request, and must notify the Administration where a ship's condition does not correspond substantially with her certificates.

blocks.h: (b) A ship classed by two societies — management and statutory responsibility — 8 marks
4. What dual class means, and why an owner takes it

blocks.p: Dual class — also called joint or double classification — is where a ship is entered with two classification societies simultaneously, and must comply with both societies' rules and hold a Certificate of Class from each. It is not the same as either of the two things candidates confuse it with:

ul: It is not transfer of class, where the ship leaves one society and joins another under the IACS transfer-of-class procedure.
It is not the ordinary and universal split between a class society and a flag Administration.

blocks.p: Owners take dual class for commercial and regulatory access rather than for safety. Typical drivers: a national requirement that ships on a particular register or in a particular domestic trade be classed with the national society; charterer or oil-major preference for a specific society; financiers or the shipyard requiring a society the owner would not otherwise use; retaining an existing society's records on a second-hand purchase while adding the buyer's preferred society; and market access to a trade where one society is dominant.
The cost is real: two rule sets to satisfy, two sets of surveys to arrange and pay for, two sets of records, and the risk that the two societies take different views of the same defect.

blocks.h: 5. How the arrangement is managed in practice

blocks.p: Management is contractual, and it is settled before the ship is entered, not after a dispute. The recurring elements are these.

ol: A joint-class agreement between the two societies and the owner. It records the scope each society takes, how surveys are shared, how findings are exchanged and how disagreement is resolved.

The stricter rule governs. Where the two rule sets differ, the ship must satisfy both, so in practice she is built and maintained to the more demanding requirement in each area. Design approval is normally led by one society with the other reviewing and accepting.

Division of the survey scope. The commonest shape is that each society surveys an agreed part of the ship — for example one taking hull and the other machinery — or that the societies alternate the survey cycle. Each then accepts the other's survey for its own class purposes.

Mutual acceptance of records. Survey reports, thickness measurement reports, conditions of class and the survey status are exchanged so that both societies' records agree. IACS procedural requirements govern this exchange between IACS members; the arrangement between an IACS and a non-IACS society is purely a matter of the agreement.

One survey status on board. The practical requirement is that the ship carries a single coherent picture of what is due and what is outstanding, whichever society raised it. Two divergent survey-status reports is the failure mode this whole arrangement exists to prevent.
Conditions of class are honoured by both. A condition imposed by either society is a condition on the ship. Clearing it with one does not clear it with the other unless the agreement so provides.

blocks.h: 6. Who conducts the statutory surveys and audits, and why this is a flag question

blocks.p: This is the part of the question that decides the mark, and the answer turns on a point of text.

Statutory surveys and audits are the flag Administration's, and only the flag Administration can say who performs them. Under regulation I/6 they are the Administration's own function; a society performs them only where that Administration has recognised and authorised it under regulation XI-1/1 and the RO Code. Dual class does not confer statutory authority on either society. A society may be the ship's classification society and have no delegation from her flag at all.

Regulation II-1/3-1 speaks of the requirements of a classification society — singular and indefinite. The construction standard is satisfied by compliance with one recognised society's requirements; nothing in the regulation contemplates or requires two.
The practical position is therefore:

ul: The Administration nominates one RO to act for it in respect of a given ship — normally one of the two societies, and normally the one it has authorised. That society issues the statutory certificates in the Administration's name.

Statutory certification is not duplicated. A ship holds one Cargo Ship Safety Construction Certificate, not two. Two societies issuing the same statutory certificate would be a defect in the delegation, not a feature of dual class.

ISM and ISPS audits follow the same rule and are separately delegated. The Administration may authorise a different organisation for audits than for surveys, and the DOC and SMC belong to the company and ship respectively, not to a class society.
The Administration may reserve items to itself — commonly initial certification, exemptions, equivalents and detention decisions — and the delegation instrument says which.

Class survey and statutory survey may be carried out by the same surveyor on the same attendance, and usually are. That convenience is exactly what obscures the distinction, and the candidate must state it: the surveyor wears two hats and acts under two different authorities.

blocks.p: Conclusion for limb (b). Dual class doubles the classification obligation and leaves the statutory obligation single. The two societies share the class work by agreement between themselves; the statutory work is performed by whichever of them — or which other organisation, or the Administration's own officers — the flag State has authorised, and by nobody else.

blocks.h: Why this structure scores

blocks.p: The question is two questions of eight marks and they are not the same kind of question. Limb (a) is a process question — it rewards a sequence, and the sequence is the ship's own life from plan approval to withdrawal of class. Limb (b) is a distinction question, and it rewards one idea held firmly: class is contractual and can be doubled; statutory authority is delegated and cannot.

Section 1 spends a short paragraph establishing that class is not law. That paragraph is what makes sections 3 and 6 scorable, because both turn on the boundary it draws. Candidates who skip it write eight marks of correct description in limb (a) and then cannot answer limb (b) at all.

blocks.h: The three capacities a classification society can occupy

blocks.p: Almost every error in this question comes from collapsing these into one. Hold them apart:

ul: Classification society — acting under its own rules, under a private contract with the owner. Sanction: condition of class, suspension, withdrawal.
Recognized Organization — acting for a flag Administration under a delegation given per SOLAS XI-1/1 and the RO Code. Sanction: the Administration's, exercised through the RO.
Nominated surveyor — an individual, not an organisation, entrusted under regulation I/6.

blocks.p: A society is not automatically an RO, is not an RO for every flag, and is not an RO for every function of a flag that has authorised it. Each of those three is a separate examinable point.

blocks.h: The textual point most candidates miss

blocks.p: SOLAS II-1/3-1 requires compliance with the requirements of a classification society recognised by the Administration. The indefinite singular is doing work: the Convention's construction standard is met by one recognised society. Dual class is therefore a commercial arrangement layered on top of a statutory scheme that neither requires it nor recognises it. Once that is seen, limb (b) writes itself.

blocks.h: Common mistakes

ul: Writing that SOLAS requires a ship to be classed. It does not. It requires compliance with a recognised society's structural, mechanical and electrical requirements or with equivalent national standards of the Administration — and the alternative is in the text.

Treating class certificates as statutory certificates. The Certificate of Class is not a Convention certificate and a port State control officer does not detain on it, though he may well ask to see the survey status.
Answering limb (b) as though dual class meant transfer of class, or as though it meant the ordinary class-and-flag split.
Saying that under dual class the two societies each issue statutory certificates. That would mean two flag delegations issuing the same certificate for the same ship.
Listing the survey types in limb (a) and never reaching plan approval, material certification or survey during construction — which is where classification actually begins.
Inventing an IACS PR number for the mutual-recognition procedure. Name the mechanism; the number is not required and a wrong one costs more than an absent one.
Forgetting that II-1/3-1 says maintained, and treating classification as a newbuilding activity that stops at delivery.

blocks.h: Examiner traps

ul: 'Who is responsible?' in limb (b) invites the answer 'the classification society'. The correct answer names the flag Administration first and the society only as its delegate.
The stem prints 'classes by two classification societies' for 'classed by'. Answer the question the examiner set; do not comment on the typography.

The word audits is in the stem alongside surveys. It is there to test whether the candidate knows ISM and ISPS audits are separately delegated and produce company and ship documents. An answer that treats 'surveys and audits' as one phrase leaves marks on the table.

'Ensuring compliance with safety and construction standards' in limb (a) is an invitation to explain the enforcement mechanism, not just to describe surveys. Conditions of class, suspension and withdrawal are the answer.

blocks.h: Likely oral follow-up

ul: Which SOLAS regulation makes class rules the construction standard, and what alternative does it allow?
Your ship is dual classed. A surveyor from society B raises a condition of class. Is it cleared when society A's surveyor is satisfied?
Who issues your Cargo Ship Safety Construction Certificate, and in whose name?
What is the difference between suspension and withdrawal of class, and what happens to your insurance in each case?
Your flag has authorised society A but not society B. Society B's surveyor attends. What can he do and what can he not do?
What is a Condition of Class and who can impose one?
Name the code that governs recognition of organisations, and say which of its parts are mandatory.

blocks.h: Memory framework

blocks.p: Limb (a) is the ship's own life: APPLY → APPROVE → CERTIFY → BUILD → ASSIGN → MAINTAIN → REPORT → CONDITION. Eight verbs, eight marks, in the order the ship experiences them.
Limb (b) is one sentence: TWO SOCIETIES, ONE FLAG. Everything about the class side doubles; nothing about the statutory side does.

blocks.p: The corpus holds no IACS document and no class rulebook (RQ-36), and its own class note is explicit that answers built on that material must be labelled class practice / IACS framework rather than presented as Convention requirements. That instruction is followed throughout limb (a) and in the management mechanics of limb (b).

The three SOLAS regulations that carry the legal weight were read at source this session from the corpus-held 2024 consolidated edition, so the load-bearing half of the answer rests on primary text and the descriptive half is honestly labelled.
No IACS procedural requirement number, no division-of-scope formula and no count of IACS members is asserted. Dual-class practice varies by agreement and no held source fixes it.

decomposition_gate.question_intent: Two eight-mark limbs of different kinds. Limb (a) is a process question about how a ship becomes and stays classed, with an explicit sub-demand about how the society ENSURES compliance - that is, its enforcement mechanism, not merely its activities. Limb (b) is a distinction question disguised as a scenario: it asks what happens when the class relationship is doubled, and then asks who does the statutory work - which is the trap, because the answer is that the statutory work was never a class function at all.
decomposition_gate.mark_allocation: 16, printed as 8 + 8. Even split, and the two limbs are genuinely equal in demand: limb (a) needs breadth across the ship's life, limb (b) needs one sharp distinction argued properly plus the practical management detail. Three sections to limb (a) and three to limb (b) gives each mark a home.
decomposition_gate.examiner_expectation: For (a): that class is a private certification against the society's own rules; the sequence from application and plan approval through material certification, construction survey, assignment with notations, the maintenance survey cycle, damage reporting and conditions of class; and that the enforcement lever is condition, suspension and withdrawal rather than detention. Then the legal hook - SOLAS II-1/3-1 adopting class rules as the construction standard, and XI-1/1 with the RO Code as the authorisation route. For (b): what dual class is and is not, why an owner takes it, the joint-class agreement and the division of survey scope, mutual acceptance of records, and above all that statutory surveys and audits belong to the flag Administration and are performed by whichever organisation it has authorised - not by both societies, and not automatically by either.
primary_source_plan: Read SOLAS II-1/3-1 at source from the corpus-held 2024 consolidated edition, because the indefinite article in it is the hinge of limb (b) and cannot be paraphrased from memory.
Read SOLAS XI-1/1 at source to establish the RO Code as the authorisation instrument and to get the mandatory/recommendatory split of its parts right.
Read SOLAS I/6 at source, because it is the regulation that makes survey the Administration's function in the first place - which is the whole of the limb (b) answer.
Read true-source/07-iacs-and-class/CLASS_AND_SURVEY_NOTES.md and obey its labelling instruction, rather than presenting class practice as Convention requirement.
Read both printed stems of QP2412-Q4 and QP2509-Q9 before deciding whether either is a donor.
Establish by corpus sweep that no IACS UR or PR text is held, so that no PR number is asserted.
decomposition_gate.freshness_risk: LOW. Every instrument used is stable across the sitting window and none was amended in it. The commercial practice described in limb (b) has no dated boundary.
decomposition_gate.jurisdiction_risk: LOW. The question is international and sets no Indian limb. The one jurisdiction-dependent element - which organisation a given flag has authorised - is stated as the rule rather than as any Administration's practice.
technical_ambiguities: 'Requirements for the classification of a ship' could mean the technical requirements the ship must meet or the procedural requirements for obtaining class. The mark allocation and the second half of the limb ('the role of classification societies in ensuring compliance') indicate the procedural reading, so the answer runs the process and states the enforcement mechanism.
'A ship is classes by two classification societies' is printed for 'classed'. Preserved verbatim; the answer treats it as 'classed'.

'Who is responsible for conducting statutory surveys and audits in such cases' presupposes that dual class changes the answer. It does not, and saying so plainly is the point of the limb rather than an evasion of it.
'Audits' is printed alongside 'surveys' and must be answered separately - ISM and ISPS verification are delegated separately and produce different documents.
decomposition_gate.target_answer_shape: Six numbered sections under two printed limb headings. Limb (a): one section drawing the class/statutory line, one running the eight-stage classification process, one on the two legal hooks and the enforcement mechanism. Limb (b): one on what dual class is and why it is taken, one on how it is managed, one on the statutory question with the II-1/3-1 textual point and a stated conclusion.

reverify_before_publication.why: Taken from SOLAS XI-1/1 read at source, which states it expressly. The RO Code itself is held but was not read paragraph by paragraph this session.

questions.understand_first: This question is really about one boundary: the line between what a classification society does for the owner under a private contract, and what it does for the flag State under a delegated statutory authority. Limb (a) is life on the owner's side of that line - how a ship becomes classed and stays classed, and what the society can actually do to an owner who lets her slip. Limb (b) then doubles the owner's side and asks what happens to the flag State's side. The answer is: nothing. Class is contractual, so a ship can have two of them; statutory authority is delegated by an Administration, so it cannot be doubled by a commercial arrangement the Administration is not party to. SOLAS II-1/3-1 makes the point in its own wording - it requires compliance with the requirements of a classification society recognised by the Administration, and one recognised society satisfies it. Everything else in this question is detail hung on that boundary.

steps.title: What classification is, and the line between class and statutory work
points: class is a private contractual certification against the society's own published rules
the society's sanction is condition, suspension and withdrawal - never detention
class is commercially compulsory even though it is not law - insurers, charterers, financiers and flag all require it
statutory work belongs to the flag Administration and reaches a society only by delegation

steps.title: The requirements a ship must satisfy to be assigned class
points: application and selection of the applicable rule set, including CSR for bulk carriers and oil tankers
plan approval of structure, machinery, piping and electrical installations before construction
approval and certification of materials and components at approved works under survey
survey during construction against the approved plans, with NDT, tank testing and trials
assignment of class and the Certificate of Class, with notations recording the basis of build
maintenance of class by annual, intermediate and renewal surveys, docking, tailshaft and machinery surveys
the owner's duty to report damage, defects and repairs affecting class
conditions of class as the time-bound instrument of enforcement short of suspension

steps.title: Where class rules acquire legal force, and how the society ensures compliance
points: SOLAS II-1/3-1 - ships shall be designed, constructed AND MAINTAINED to the requirements of a recognised society, or to equivalent national standards
SOLAS I/6 - survey is the Administration's function, which it may entrust to nominated surveyors or recognized organizations
SOLAS XI-1/1 - that authorisation must follow the RO Code, MSC.349(92), parts 1 and 2 mandatory
the society acts in two capacities - as class under its own rules, and as RO in the Administration's name
the RO's minimum powers under I/6 - require repairs, survey at a port State's request, notify the Administration

steps.title: What dual class means, and why an owner takes it
points: entered with two societies at once; both rule sets must be satisfied and two Certificates of Class held
distinguish sharply from transfer of class and from the ordinary class/flag split
drivers - national register requirements, charterer or oil-major preference, yard or financier requirement, second-hand purchase, market access
costs - two rule sets, two survey programmes, two record sets, and the risk of divergent views

steps.title: How the arrangement is managed in practice
points: a joint-class agreement settled in advance between the two societies and the owner
where the rule sets differ the stricter governs, because both must be satisfied
division of the survey scope - by system, or by alternating the cycle - with each accepting the other's survey
mutual exchange and acceptance of survey reports, thickness measurements and conditions of class
one coherent survey status on board, whichever society raised the item

steps.title: Who conducts the statutory surveys and audits, and why this is a flag question
points: statutory surveys and audits are the Administration's; only it can say who performs them
dual class confers no statutory authority - a society may class the ship and hold no delegation from her flag
SOLAS II-1/3-1 speaks of A classification society - singular and indefinite; one recognised society satisfies it
statutory certification is not duplicated - one Cargo Ship Safety Construction Certificate, not two
ISM and ISPS audits are separately delegated and produce the DOC and SMC and the ISSC
the same surveyor may do both on one attendance, under two different authorities - which is what obscures the distinction

questions.memory_cue: Two sentences carry the whole answer. Limb (a) is the ship's own life — APPLY, APPROVE, CERTIFY, BUILD, ASSIGN, MAINTAIN, REPORT, CONDITION (2), with the law bolted on at step (3). Limb (b) is four words — TWO SOCIETIES, ONE FLAG (6).

quick_revision.recall_15s: Class is a private contract; statutory authority is a flag delegation. Class runs APPLY → APPROVE → CERTIFY → BUILD → ASSIGN → MAINTAIN → REPORT → CONDITION, enforced by condition of class, suspension and withdrawal. SOLAS II-1/3-1 makes a recognised society's rules the construction standard; I/6 makes survey the Administration's; XI-1/1 plus the RO Code (MSC.349(92)) is how it is delegated. Dual class doubles the class side and nothing else — two rule sets, two Certificates of Class, one flag, one set of statutory certificates.
critical_numbers: RO Code MSC.349(92) - parts 1 and 2 MANDATORY, part 3 RECOMMENDATORY
Renewal survey cycle 5 years, with annual and intermediate surveys between
Dual class: 2 rule sets, 2 Certificates of Class, 1 flag Administration, 1 set of statutory certificates
quick_revision.critical_regulation: SOLAS II-1/3-1 read with XI-1/1 and I/6. II-1/3-1 adopts the requirements of a classification society recognised by the Administration as the construction standard, and requires the ship to be designed, constructed and maintained to them; I/6 makes inspection and survey the Administration's own function with a power to entrust it; XI-1/1 requires any such authorisation to be given in accordance with the RO Code.
quick_revision.major_trap: Answering limb (b) with 'the classification societies do the statutory surveys'. Statutory surveys and audits belong to the flag Administration, and a society performs them only where that Administration has recognised and authorised it. Dual class is an arrangement between the owner and two societies; the flag State is not a party to it and its delegation is unaffected by it.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Give the route for the classification and dual-class question.
retrieval_cards.answer: (a) 1 What class is, and the class/statutory line. 2 The eight-stage classification process. 3 Where class rules acquire legal force, and the enforcement mechanism. (b) 4 What dual class is and why it is taken. 5 How it is managed. 6 Who does the statutory surveys and audits.
retrieval_cards.why: Three sections per limb match the 8 + 8 split, and section 1 is what makes section 6 arguable rather than asserted.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Which SOLAS regulation makes class rules the construction standard, and what alternative does it allow?
retrieval_cards.answer: Regulation II-1/3-1. Ships shall be designed, constructed and maintained in compliance with the structural, mechanical and electrical requirements of a classification society recognised by the Administration under regulation XI-1/1 - or with applicable national standards of the Administration providing an equivalent level of safety. The alternative is in the text, so SOLAS does not strictly require class.
retrieval_cards.why: Candidates routinely write that SOLAS requires classification. It does not, and the exception is examinable.

retrieval_cards.prompt: In what two capacities can a classification society act, and what is the sanction in each?
retrieval_cards.answer: As classification society under its own rules, by private contract with the owner - sanction: condition of class, suspension, withdrawal. As Recognized Organization under a flag Administration's delegation given per SOLAS XI-1/1 and the RO Code - it issues statutory certificates in the Administration's name and exercises the Administration's authority.
retrieval_cards.why: The whole of limb (b) depends on holding these apart, and the same surveyor often performs both on one attendance.

retrieval_cards.prompt: What is dual class, and what is it not?
retrieval_cards.answer: A ship entered with two classification societies at the same time, complying with both rule sets and holding a Certificate of Class from each. It is not transfer of class - leaving one society for another - and it is not the ordinary split between class society and flag Administration.
retrieval_cards.why: Both confusions are common and either one loses the whole limb.

retrieval_cards.prompt: A ship is dual classed. Who issues her statutory certificates?
retrieval_cards.answer: Whichever organisation the flag Administration has recognised and authorised for that ship - normally one of the two societies, possibly neither, or the Administration's own officers. Statutory certification is not duplicated: one Cargo Ship Safety Construction Certificate, not two. Dual class confers no statutory authority on either society.
retrieval_cards.why: This is the mark-deciding point of limb (b) and the trap the stem is built around.

retrieval_cards.prompt: How is a dual-class arrangement managed?
retrieval_cards.answer: By a joint-class agreement settled in advance: the scope each society takes, how surveys are shared, how records are exchanged, how disagreement is resolved. Where the rule sets differ the stricter governs, because both must be satisfied. Survey scope is divided by system or by alternating the cycle, each society accepting the other's survey, with one coherent survey status carried on board.
retrieval_cards.why: The stem asks 'how is this process managed', which is a procedure demand, not a definition demand.

retrieval_cards.prompt: List the stages by which a ship becomes and remains classed.
retrieval_cards.answer: Application and rule selection; plan approval; approval and certification of materials and components; survey during construction; assignment of class with notations and the Certificate of Class; maintenance of class by the survey cycle; reporting of damage, defects and repairs; conditions of class where compliance is impaired.
retrieval_cards.why: Eight stages for eight marks, in the order the ship experiences them.

retrieval_cards.prompt: What does the RO Code do, and which of its parts are mandatory?
retrieval_cards.answer: It sets what an organisation must be and must do to be recognised and authorised by an Administration, and how the Administration must oversee it. Resolution MSC.349(92): parts 1 and 2 are mandatory, part 3 is recommendatory. SOLAS XI-1/1 requires authorisation to be given in accordance with it.
retrieval_cards.why: The mandatory/recommendatory split is a precise, checkable fact and is stated in XI-1/1 itself.

retrieval_cards.prompt: The stem says 'statutory surveys and audits'. Why are audits mentioned separately?
retrieval_cards.answer: Because ISM and ISPS verification is delegated separately from survey and produces different documents - the Document of Compliance to the company, the Safety Management Certificate and the International Ship Security Certificate to the ship. An Administration may authorise a different organisation for audits than for surveys.
retrieval_cards.why: Treating 'surveys and audits' as one phrase leaves an examinable distinction unanswered.

blocks.h: 1. The definition - and it is printed twice, not once

blocks.p: Substantial corrosion is defined in the 2011 ESP Code (resolution A.1049(27), mandatory through SOLAS regulation XI-1/2), at paragraph 1.2.9. The Code gives two definitions and a Class I answer gives both.

ol: The general definition. Substantial corrosion is an extent of corrosion such that assessment of the corrosion pattern indicates wastage in excess of 75 per cent of allowable margins, but within acceptable limits.

The Common Structural Rules definition. For ships built under the IACS Common Structural Rules, substantial corrosion is an extent of corrosion such that assessment of the corrosion pattern indicates a gauged (or measured) thickness between t-net + 0.5 mm and t-net.

blocks.p: Read the general definition carefully, because both halves of it are examinable. 'In excess of 75 per cent of allowable margins' means most — but not all — of the corrosion allowance is gone. 'But within acceptable limits' means the structure is still acceptable. Substantial corrosion is therefore not a defect requiring immediate renewal. It is a warning state: a declaration that this location is close to its limit and must now be watched more closely and measured more widely.

The CSR definition says the same thing in a different currency. Under CSR the scantling is expressed as a net thickness plus a corrosion addition; substantial corrosion is the last 0.5 mm above the net thickness. Below t-net the steel is no longer acceptable at all.

blocks.h: 2. Where the concept sits, and the model it presupposes

blocks.p: The definition only makes sense against the corrosion-allowance model of hull scantlings, and stating that model first is what converts a memorised sentence into an answer.

ul: A rule scantling is a net thickness required for strength, plus a corrosion addition for the wastage expected over the ship's life.
Allowable margin is that addition. Renewal thickness is the point at which it is exhausted and the steel must be renewed.
Wastage is therefore measured not as a percentage of the original plate but as a proportion of the margin. Substantial corrosion is 75 per cent of the way through it.

blocks.p: The Code is deliberate about its own status. Paragraph 1.1.3 states that it contains the minimum extent of examination, thickness measurement and tank testing, and that 'the survey should be extended when substantial corrosion and/or structural defects are found and include additional close-up survey when necessary'. That sentence is the engine of the whole question: a finding of substantial corrosion is the trigger that enlarges the survey.

One further consequence is easy to miss. Paragraph 1.2.2 provides that a space used for both cargo and salt water ballast is treated as a ballast tank when substantial corrosion has been found in it. A finding does not merely add measurements — it can change the survey regime the space falls under.

blocks.h: 3. The criteria used to assess it during inspections

blocks.p: The surveyor is not applying one criterion but a small set, and the Code supplies the vocabulary for each.

ol: The measured wastage against the allowable margin. The primary criterion. The gauged thickness is compared with the rule renewal thickness taken from the society's rules and the ship's approved scantling drawings; the result is expressed as a proportion of the margin, and 75 per cent is the threshold.

The corrosion pattern, not a single reading. The Code says 'assessment of the corrosion pattern'. A single low point is not the test. General diminution, grooving, pitting and edge and weld-line wastage are read together across the member.

Coating condition, graded by paragraph 1.2.11 as GOOD (only minor spot rusting), FAIR (local breakdown at edges of stiffeners and weld connections, and/or light rusting over 20 per cent or more of the areas under consideration, but less than POOR) or POOR (general breakdown of coating over 20 per cent or more of areas, or hard scale at 10 per cent or more). Coating condition is what tells the surveyor where corrosion will appear next.

Whether a corrosion prevention system is in place and effective. Paragraph 1.2.10 treats a corrosion prevention system as normally a full hard protective coating, usually epoxy or equivalent. A tank with no effective system attracts a heavier survey regardless of today's measurements.

Whether the location is a suspect area. Paragraph 1.2.8: suspect areas are locations showing substantial corrosion and/or considered by the surveyor to be prone to rapid wastage. Note the 'and/or' — the surveyor's judgement is an independent route into the category.

The ship's history. Paragraph 1.2.7 requires that in selecting representative spaces, account be taken of the service and repair history and of identifiable critical or suspect areas. Previous findings drive present scope.

blocks.h: 4. Inspection techniques - how it is actually found

blocks.p: The techniques run from the general to the particular, and the Code's own sequence is the right order to write them in.

ol: Preparation. The space must be cleaned, de-scaled, ventilated, gas-freed, illuminated and made safe for access. A poorly prepared tank is the commonest reason a survey cannot be credited.
Overall survey — a survey to report on the overall condition of the hull structure and to determine the extent of additional close-up surveys required.

Close-up survey — defined at paragraph 1.2.5 as a survey where the details of structural components are within the close visual inspection range of the surveyor, normally within reach of hand. Achieved by staging, rafting, cherry-picker, rope access or remote inspection techniques as the society accepts.

Thickness measurement by ultrasonic gauging, carried out by a company certified for the purpose — the Code carries a dedicated annex of procedures for certification of a company engaged in thickness measurement of hull structures — and witnessed by the attending surveyor.

Simultaneity. Paragraph 1.5 requires that, in any kind of survey, thickness measurements of structures in areas where close-up surveys are required be carried out simultaneously with the close-up surveys. Measuring after the staging has come down is not compliance.

Supplementary techniques where the visual and gauged evidence points to cracking rather than wastage: magnetic particle or dye-penetrant inspection at weld toes and hard spots, and hammer testing to identify heavily scaled or grooved material.
Tank pressure testing of boundaries, and internal examination of the spaces the Code lists.
Recording. Thickness measurement reports on the Code's reporting format, the survey report, and the Condition Evaluation Report which summarises the ship's structural condition at the renewal survey.

blocks.h: 5. What a finding does to the renewal survey

blocks.p: The renewal survey is the five-yearly hull survey that re-establishes fitness for the next period of validity of the Cargo Ship Safety Construction Certificate. Its shape is fixed before substantial corrosion is found, and is then enlarged by the finding.

The baseline. Under section 2, the renewal survey may commence at the fourth annual survey and be progressed during the succeeding year with a view to completion by the fifth anniversary date (2.1.1); the survey programme is dealt with in advance and thickness measurement is not to be held before the fourth annual survey (2.1.2); all cargo holds, ballast tanks, pipe tunnels, cofferdams and void spaces bounding cargo holds, decks and the outer hull are examined and the examination supplemented by thickness measurement and testing, sufficient to discover substantial corrosion, significant deformation, fractures, damage or other structural deterioration (2.1.4); a dry-dock survey forms part of it, with a minimum of two bottom inspections in the five-year period and a maximum interval of 36 months, in dry-dock for ships of 15 years and over (2.2.1–2.2.2); and concurrent crediting to both the intermediate and the renewal survey is not acceptable (2.1.7).
The steps once substantial corrosion is found:

ol: Extend the thickness measurements to the increased extent the Code's dedicated annex prescribes for areas of substantial corrosion. The Code is express, in the corresponding intermediate-survey provision, that these extended measurements must be carried out before the survey is credited as completed — the survey is not closed on a promise.
Extend the close-up survey where necessary, per paragraph 1.1.3, to establish the extent of the affected structure rather than the extent of the first sample.

Record the locations as suspect areas, so that they are examined at every subsequent survey and gauged again. This is the mechanism by which a single finding follows the ship for the rest of her life.
Re-classify the space where 1.2.2 applies, so that a combined cargo and ballast space is thereafter surveyed as a ballast tank.

Assess against renewal thickness. Where measurements are within the substantial-corrosion band the steel is acceptable but monitored; where they are at or below renewal thickness the material must be dealt with now.
Repair or renew, to an approved scheme — section 6 below.

Deal with the cause, not only the symptom. Coating condition graded POOR, a failed or absent corrosion prevention system, or defective anodes are addressed as part of the same event, because renewing steel into a failed coating simply restarts the clock.
Complete the records — thickness measurement reports, survey report and Condition Evaluation Report — and only then credit the survey.

blocks.h: 6. Repair methods and their acceptance

blocks.p: This part of the answer is class practice and the IACS framework, not Convention text, and should be written as such. What the ESP Code supplies is the trigger and the record; what the society's rules supply is the acceptance.

ul: Cropping and renewal of wasted plating and stiffening is the primary and permanent remedy: the wasted material is cut out and replaced with new material of at least the original rule thickness, of approved grade, with approved welding procedures, qualified welders and approved consumables, and with post-weld NDT.
Partial renewal — renewing the wasted strake, face plate, web or bracket rather than the whole member — where the wastage is local and the surrounding structure is sound.
Insert plates with full penetration butt welds, sized and positioned so that seams do not fall in high-stress locations or coincide with existing welds.

Doubler plates are a temporary and conditional measure only, accepted at the society's discretion, usually with a time limit and a condition of class requiring permanent repair. A doubler conceals the parent material and traps moisture behind it, which is precisely why it is not a repair.
Weld repair and build-up for grooving corrosion along weld lines, within the limits the society allows — it is easy to do more harm than good by heat input into thin material.
Renewal of the corrosion prevention system: surface preparation, coating to the maker's specification, and renewal of sacrificial anodes.
Reinforcement or redesign where wastage is recurrent in the same location, because a repeated failure is a design or drainage problem rather than a maintenance one.

blocks.p: Two conditions govern all of it. First, a repair affecting classed structure requires the society's prior approval of the repair scheme and survey of the completed work. Second, the work must be recorded, because the next surveyor's scope depends on knowing what was done.

blocks.h: 7. The role of the classification society

blocks.p: The society is present at every stage of what has just been described, and it is worth naming the roles separately because they are different.

ol: Rule-maker. It sets the scantlings, the corrosion additions and the renewal thicknesses against which everything is measured, and adopts the IACS Unified Requirements and the Common Structural Rules into its own rules.
Survey planner. It agrees the survey programme in advance with the owner, and it determines the extent of close-up survey and thickness measurement — including the extension the finding requires.
Attending surveyor. It carries out the overall and close-up surveys, witnesses the gauging and applies the assessment criteria in section 3.
Approver of the repair. It approves the repair scheme, the materials, the welding procedures and the welders, and surveys the completed repair.
Keeper of the record. It maintains the survey status, the thickness measurement records, the Condition Evaluation Report and the suspect-area register that determines future survey scope.

Enforcer. Where compliance is impaired it imposes a condition of class with a due date; if that is not cleared, class is suspended. Because the Cargo Ship Safety Construction Certificate is normally issued by the same organisation acting as the flag State's Recognized Organization, the practical consequence reaches the ship's statutory certification too — but through the flag State's delegation, not through class itself.

Certifier of the measuring company. The Code's own annex requires the thickness-measurement company to be certified, and that certification is a class function — a point almost no candidate makes and one that shows the whole chain has been understood.

blocks.h: Why this structure scores

blocks.p: The stem asks four things in one sentence — define, criteria, steps at renewal survey, and within that inspection techniques, repair methods and the role of class. The commonest failure is to write a good definition and then a vague paragraph about surveys, which collects perhaps five of sixteen marks. Seven sections in the printed order of the demands guarantee that every demand has a home, and the definition section is deliberately short so that the procedural sections can be full.

The single most valuable thing in this answer is the observation in section 1 that substantial corrosion is a warning state, not a defect. It follows straight from the Code's own words 'but within acceptable limits', and it explains why the correct response is to measure more rather than to renew. A candidate who writes 'substantial corrosion means the plate must be renewed' has contradicted the definition he just quoted.

blocks.h: The two definitions, side by side

rows: Wastage in excess of 75% of allowable margins
Gauged thickness between t-net + 0.5 mm and t-net
A proportion of the corrosion allowance
An absolute band above the net thickness
At or below renewal thickness: renew

blocks.p: Both are printed in ESP Code paragraph 1.2.9. Quoting only the first is the commonest incompleteness in this answer, and the CSR limb is the more likely one on a modern bulk carrier or tanker.

blocks.h: The corrosion-allowance model, in one line

blocks.p: Rule scantling = net thickness + corrosion addition. The addition is the allowable margin. Substantial corrosion is 75 per cent of the way through the addition — not 75 per cent of the plate. A candidate who says 'more than 75 per cent of the plate thickness is gone' has described a hole, not substantial corrosion, and has lost the definition mark.

blocks.h: What triggers what

rows: Thickness measurements extended to the annex extent; close-up survey extended as necessary (1.1.3)
Survey not credited as completed until they are done
Becomes a suspect area (1.2.8) - examined and gauged at every later survey
Combined cargo/ballast space with substantial corrosion
Treated as a ballast tank thereafter (1.2.2)
Heavier survey regime; the coating itself must be dealt with
No longer substantial corrosion - the steel is unacceptable and must be renewed

blocks.h: Common mistakes

ul: Giving only one of the two definitions in paragraph 1.2.9.
Saying substantial corrosion means 75 per cent of the plate thickness is lost, rather than 75 per cent of the allowable margin.
Treating substantial corrosion as a defect requiring immediate renewal, which contradicts 'but within acceptable limits'.
Describing the renewal survey generically and never saying what the finding changes — which is the actual question.
Omitting that extended measurements must be completed before the survey is credited.
Offering doubler plates as a repair method without saying they are temporary, conditional and normally attract a condition of class.
Attributing the ESP Code to SOLAS chapter II-1. It is made mandatory by SOLAS XI-1/2.
Presenting repair acceptance criteria as Convention requirements. They are class rules.
Quoting a numeric renewal thickness. It is rule- and ship-specific and inventing one is worse than giving the method.

blocks.h: Examiner traps

ul: 'Define' is the first word of the stem. An approximate paraphrase will not do; the two-limb definition is the cheapest three marks on the paper and the most commonly half-taken.

'What criteria are used' is plural and is not a repeat of the definition. It wants the assessment framework: pattern rather than point, coating condition, corrosion prevention system, suspect-area status and survey history.

'Including inspection techniques, repair methods, and the role of the classification society' is a three-part instruction embedded in a clause. Each of the three is worth marks and each needs its own section.
The ESP Code applies to bulk carriers and oil tankers. Saying so is a mark; silently generalising the definition to all ships is a small error a strong examiner will notice.

The Code's language is 'should' throughout, because it is a code applied through class and made mandatory by SOLAS XI-1/2 rather than drafted as SOLAS text. Reproducing it as 'shall' misstates the instrument.

blocks.h: Likely oral follow-up

ul: Define substantial corrosion. Now give the Common Structural Rules definition.
Is a plate in substantial corrosion acceptable? Then why does it matter?
You find substantial corrosion in a topside tank at the fourth annual survey. What happens to the scope of the renewal survey?
What is a suspect area, and how does a location become one?
Grade this coating: local breakdown at stiffener edges with light rusting over about a quarter of the area.
Who is allowed to take the thickness measurements, and who witnesses them?
Your owner asks for a doubler plate over a wasted strake. What do you tell him?
Which instrument makes the ESP Code mandatory?
What is in the Condition Evaluation Report, and why does the next surveyor want it?

blocks.h: Memory framework

blocks.p: The answer is the surveyor's own working day: DEFINE → MODEL → CRITERIA → FIND → EXTEND → FIX → CLASS. Seven words, seven sections.
For the definition itself, one sentence: seventy-five per cent of the margin, still acceptable, so measure more. It contains the number, the caveat and the consequence.

blocks.h: Regulation and source map

rows: Suspect areas - and the surveyor's independent judgement route
Coating condition GOOD / FAIR / POOR with the 20% and 10% figures
Corrosion prevention system as a full hard protective coating
The Code is a minimum; the survey is extended when substantial corrosion is found
Thickness measurement simultaneous with close-up survey
A combined space becomes a ballast tank once substantial corrosion is found
The renewal survey - timing, scope, dry-dock, no concurrent crediting
Extended measurement extent; certification of the measuring company; Condition Evaluation Report
Renewal thickness, repair acceptance, welding approval

blocks.h: Uncertainty and currency

blocks.p: The corpus holds the base 2011 ESP Code and its instrument log records expressly that the amendment chain after A.1049(27) is not assembled (RQ-26), the Code being amended at almost every MSC session. Everything cited in this answer is read from the base text and no amendment is asserted. For a definition-and-procedure question that is sufficient; for an edition-precise citation it would not be, and the log says so.

The annex that carries the extended measurement extent is numbered differently in the bulk carrier and oil tanker annexes of the Code, so it is named here by its function rather than by a number that would be right for only one ship type.

No numeric renewal thickness, corrosion addition or acceptance criterion for doubler plates is quoted. Those are rule- and ship-specific, the corpus holds no class rulebook, and the method is worth more to a candidate than a figure that would be wrong for his ship.

decomposition_gate.question_intent: One 16-mark question carrying four sequential demands in a single printed sentence: define the term; state the criteria by which it is assessed; discuss the steps taken to address it at a renewal survey; and within that last demand cover inspection techniques, repair methods and the role of the classification society. It is a definition-plus-procedure question, and the definition is the smallest part of it.
decomposition_gate.mark_allocation: 16, undivided. The printed demands imply roughly 3 for the definition, 3 for the criteria and 10 across the renewal-survey material, of which the three named sub-demands take most. Seven sections weight it that way: sections 1 and 2 are compact, sections 3 to 7 carry the bulk.
decomposition_gate.examiner_expectation: The ESP Code definition - and ideally both limbs of it, including the Common Structural Rules form. Then the corrosion-allowance model that makes the 75 per cent figure meaningful. Then the assessment criteria: pattern rather than single reading, coating condition in the Code's three grades, whether a corrosion prevention system is present and effective, suspect-area status and survey history. Then the renewal survey - its baseline timing and scope, and specifically what the finding changes: extended thickness measurement to the annex extent, extended close-up survey, recording as suspect areas, completion before crediting. Then repair by cropping and renewal with doublers correctly characterised as temporary. Then class as rule-maker, planner, surveyor, approver of repairs, record-keeper, enforcer and certifier of the measuring company.
primary_source_plan: Read paragraph 1.2.9 of the ESP Code at source from the corpus-held A.1049(27), because the definition is the first word of the stem and a paraphrase will not score.
Read the surrounding definitions 1.2.2, 1.2.5 to 1.2.8, 1.2.10 and 1.2.11 at source, because the criteria demand is answered from them and the coating grades carry checkable numbers.
Read 1.1.3 and 1.5 at source to establish the extension trigger and the simultaneity requirement, which are the two provisions that convert a finding into survey work.
Read section 2 at source for the renewal survey baseline, and the intermediate-survey provision that states extended measurements must precede crediting.
Read the Code's own contents page for the annex that carries the extended-measurement extent, and confirm whether its number is common to both annexes before citing it.
Read the corpus ESP instrument log and carry its RQ-26 completeness position forward rather than asserting a current edition.
Read the corpus class note and obey its labelling instruction for the repair-acceptance material.
decomposition_gate.freshness_risk: LOW for the definition and the survey architecture, which have been stable since 2011. MEDIUM only in the sense that the Code is frequently amended and the corpus does not hold the chain - which is handled by asserting nothing that depends on a post-2011 change.
decomposition_gate.jurisdiction_risk: LOW. The ESP Code is international and operates through class and the flag Administration. No Indian limb is set.
technical_ambiguities: 'In the context of ship structure and classification requirements' signals that the class definition is wanted rather than a general corrosion-engineering description. The answer leads with the Code definition.

'Criteria used to assess' could be read as a restatement of the definition. It is not: the definition is the threshold, the criteria are how the surveyor decides the threshold is met - which is why they are given a separate section.
'Steps taken to address substantial corrosion during a renewal survey' could be read as repair only. The Code's own answer is broader: the first step is to measure more, not to repair.
The Code prints 'should' rather than 'shall'. Reproduced as the Code prints it, with its mandatory route through SOLAS XI-1/2 stated separately.
The extended-measurement annex is numbered differently in the bulk carrier and oil tanker annexes, so it is cited by function rather than by number.
decomposition_gate.target_answer_shape: Seven numbered sections following the printed demands. Two compact ones - the two-limb definition, then the corrosion-allowance model with the extension trigger. Then the criteria as a numbered set drawn from the Code's own definitions. Then inspection techniques in the surveyor's working order. Then the renewal survey baseline followed by an explicit list of what the finding changes. Then repair methods, labelled class practice, with doublers correctly qualified. Then the society's seven distinct roles.

reverify_before_publication.claim: Every ESP Code paragraph number and quotation used in this answer
reverify_before_publication.why: Read at source from the base text of A.1049(27), which the corpus holds. The corpus instrument log records the amendment chain after A.1049(27) as not assembled (RQ-26) and the Code is amended at almost every MSC session, so a later renumbering of a cited paragraph cannot be excluded from held sources.

reverify_before_publication.claim: Repair methods and their acceptance - cropping and renewal, insert plates, doubler plates as a temporary measure, weld build-up, and the requirement for approved procedures and welders
reverify_before_publication.why: Class practice and the IACS framework. The corpus holds no IACS UR and no class rulebook (RQ-36) and its class note requires this labelling. No society's acceptance criterion is asserted.

reverify_before_publication.claim: The corrosion-allowance model - rule scantling as net thickness plus corrosion addition, with renewal thickness at its exhaustion
reverify_before_publication.why: The model the Code's own definition presupposes, and it is stated in the CSR limb of 1.2.9 in t-net terms. The general-rule expression of it is class practice and no rulebook is held, so no numeric addition or renewal thickness is quoted.

questions.understand_first: The examiner is testing whether you understand that substantial corrosion is a warning, not a failure. The ESP Code's own words are 'wastage in excess of 75 per cent of allowable margins, but within acceptable limits' — the steel is still good. What has been consumed is most of the corrosion allowance, the margin deliberately added to the net scantling to be eaten over the ship's life. So the correct response to a finding is not to cut plate out; it is to find out how far it goes. That is why the Code makes the finding a trigger that enlarges the survey — more thickness measurement, more close-up survey, and the location placed on a suspect-area register that follows the ship for the rest of her life. Renewal only enters when the measurements reach the renewal thickness, at which point the material is no longer in substantial corrosion at all: it is simply unacceptable. Hold that logic and the whole answer — criteria, techniques, steps, repairs and the society's role — falls out of it in order.

steps.title: The definition - and it is printed twice, not once
points: ESP Code A.1049(27) paragraph 1.2.9, mandatory through SOLAS XI-1/2
general definition - wastage in excess of 75 per cent of allowable margins, but within acceptable limits
IACS CSR definition - gauged thickness between t-net + 0.5 mm and t-net
'but within acceptable limits' means the steel is still acceptable: this is a warning state, not a defect

steps.title: Where the concept sits, and the model it presupposes
points: rule scantling equals net thickness plus corrosion addition; the addition is the allowable margin
renewal thickness is the point at which the margin is exhausted
paragraph 1.1.3 - the Code is a MINIMUM and the survey is extended when substantial corrosion is found
paragraph 1.2.2 - a combined cargo and ballast space becomes a ballast tank once substantial corrosion is found there

steps.title: The criteria used to assess it during inspections
points: measured wastage against the rule renewal thickness, expressed as a proportion of the margin
the corrosion PATTERN, not a single low reading
coating condition graded GOOD, FAIR or POOR under paragraph 1.2.11, with the 20 per cent and 10 per cent thresholds
whether a corrosion prevention system is present and effective, per 1.2.10
suspect-area status under 1.2.8 - including the surveyor's independent judgement route
the ship's service and repair history, per 1.2.7

steps.title: Inspection techniques - how it is actually found
points: preparation - cleaning, de-scaling, ventilation, gas-freeing, lighting and safe access
overall survey to determine the extent of additional close-up survey
close-up survey - within close visual inspection range, normally within reach of hand (1.2.5)
ultrasonic thickness measurement by a certified company, witnessed by the surveyor
paragraph 1.5 - measurement simultaneous with the close-up survey
MPI or dye penetrant where cracking rather than wastage is suspected; hammer testing
tank pressure testing, and recording through the thickness measurement report and Condition Evaluation Report

steps.title: What a finding does to the renewal survey
points: the baseline - may commence at the fourth annual and complete by the fifth anniversary (2.1.1)
scope under 2.1.4, sufficient to DISCOVER substantial corrosion; dry-dock survey part of it; no concurrent crediting (2.1.7)
extend thickness measurement to the annex extent, and complete it BEFORE the survey is credited
extend close-up survey to establish the true extent of the affected structure
record the locations as suspect areas so they follow the ship
assess against renewal thickness, and deal with the cause - coating and anodes - not only the symptom

steps.title: Repair methods and their acceptance
points: cropping and renewal as the primary permanent remedy, with approved procedures, welders and consumables and post-weld NDT
partial renewal and insert plates with full penetration welds, sited clear of high-stress locations
doubler plates as a TEMPORARY and CONDITIONAL measure only, normally with a condition of class
weld repair and build-up for grooving corrosion, within the society's limits
renewal of the corrosion prevention system and anodes
prior approval of the repair scheme and survey of the completed work

steps.title: The role of the classification society
points: rule-maker - scantlings, corrosion additions, renewal thicknesses, and adoption of IACS URs and CSR
survey planner - the survey programme agreed in advance, and the extent of close-up survey and gauging

approver of the repair scheme, materials, welding procedures and welders

questions.memory_cue: The surveyor's working day, in seven words — DEFINE (1), MODEL (2), CRITERIA (3), FIND (4), EXTEND (5), FIX (6), CLASS (7). For the definition itself: seventy-five per cent of the margin, still acceptable, so measure more.

quick_revision.recall_15s: ESP Code A.1049(27) para 1.2.9, mandatory via SOLAS XI-1/2. Substantial corrosion = wastage in excess of 75% of allowable margins, but within acceptable limits; under IACS CSR, gauged thickness between t-net + 0.5 mm and t-net. It is a warning state, not a defect. Consequence: extend thickness measurement and close-up survey (1.1.3), complete the extension before crediting the survey, and record the location as a suspect area (1.2.8). Renew only at renewal thickness. Coating graded GOOD / FAIR / POOR (1.2.11).
critical_numbers: Substantial corrosion: wastage in excess of 75% of allowable margins, but within acceptable limits
IACS CSR form: gauged thickness between t-net + 0.5 mm and t-net
Coating POOR: general breakdown over 20% or more of areas, or hard scale at 10% or more
Coating FAIR: local breakdown at stiffener edges and weld connections and/or light rusting over 20% or more, but less than POOR
Renewal survey may commence at the 4th annual survey and complete by the 5th anniversary; thickness measurement not before the 4th annual
Dry-dock: minimum 2 bottom inspections in the 5-year period, maximum interval 36 months; in dry-dock for ships 15 years and over
quick_revision.critical_regulation: 2011 ESP Code, resolution A.1049(27), made mandatory by SOLAS regulation XI-1/2. Paragraph 1.2.9 carries both definitions; paragraph 1.1.3 makes the Code a minimum and requires the survey to be extended when substantial corrosion is found; paragraph 1.2.8 turns the location into a suspect area for every later survey.
quick_revision.major_trap: Saying that substantial corrosion means the plate must be renewed, or that 75 per cent of the plate thickness has been lost. Neither is what the Code says. It is 75 per cent of the allowable margin — the corrosion addition, not the plate — and the Code adds 'but within acceptable limits', so the steel is still acceptable. The required response is to measure more widely, not to cut it out.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Define substantial corrosion, in both forms the ESP Code prints.
retrieval_cards.answer: ESP Code paragraph 1.2.9. General: an extent of corrosion such that assessment of the corrosion pattern indicates wastage in excess of 75 per cent of allowable margins, but within acceptable limits. For ships built under the IACS Common Structural Rules: an extent of corrosion such that assessment of the corrosion pattern indicates a gauged (or measured) thickness between t-net + 0.5 mm and t-net.
retrieval_cards.why: The stem opens with 'Define'. Giving only the general limb is the commonest incompleteness, and the CSR limb is the more likely one on a modern bulk carrier or tanker.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Substantial corrosion has been found. Must the plate be renewed?
retrieval_cards.answer: No. The definition ends 'but within acceptable limits' — the steel is still acceptable. The required response is to extend the thickness measurements and, where necessary, the close-up survey, and to record the location as a suspect area. Renewal is required only when measurements reach the renewal thickness, at which point the material is no longer in substantial corrosion but simply unacceptable.
retrieval_cards.why: The single most valuable point in the answer, and it follows from the definition the candidate has just quoted.

retrieval_cards.prompt: State the three coating condition grades and their numeric thresholds.
retrieval_cards.answer: ESP Code 1.2.11. GOOD — only minor spot rusting. FAIR — local breakdown at edges of stiffeners and weld connections and/or light rusting over 20 per cent or more of areas under consideration, but less than POOR. POOR — general breakdown of coating over 20 per cent or more of areas, or hard scale at 10 per cent or more of areas.
retrieval_cards.why: Two checkable numbers in one definition, and coating condition is one of the assessment criteria the stem asks for.

retrieval_cards.prompt: What is a suspect area, and how does a location become one?
retrieval_cards.answer: ESP Code 1.2.8: locations showing substantial corrosion and/or considered by the surveyor to be prone to rapid wastage. Note the 'and/or' — the surveyor's judgement is an independent route in, without any measurement. Once recorded, the location is examined and gauged at every subsequent survey.
retrieval_cards.why: This is the mechanism by which one finding follows the ship for life, and the 'and/or' is a precise point most candidates miss.

retrieval_cards.prompt: What changes at a renewal survey once substantial corrosion is found?
retrieval_cards.answer: Extend the thickness measurements to the extent the Code's dedicated annex prescribes, and complete them before the survey is credited. Extend the close-up survey as necessary (1.1.3). Record the locations as suspect areas (1.2.8). Re-classify a combined cargo/ballast space as a ballast tank (1.2.2). Assess against renewal thickness, repair or renew where it is reached, and deal with the coating and anodes as well as the steel.
retrieval_cards.why: This is the core of the stem's third demand and the part most often answered generically.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Which instrument makes the ESP Code mandatory, and what is the Code's own status?
retrieval_cards.answer: SOLAS regulation XI-1/2 makes the 2011 ESP Code (resolution A.1049(27)) mandatory. The Code itself is written in 'should' language and sets the minimum extent of examination, thickness measurement and tank testing — paragraph 1.1.3 — which is why the survey is extended, not reduced, when substantial corrosion is found.
retrieval_cards.why: Attributing the ESP Code to SOLAS chapter II-1 is a common and avoidable error, and the 'minimum' point sets up the whole answer.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Your owner proposes a doubler plate over a wasted strake. What is the correct answer?
retrieval_cards.answer: A doubler is a temporary and conditional measure only, accepted at the society's discretion, normally time-limited and normally attracting a condition of class requiring permanent repair. It conceals the parent material from inspection and traps moisture behind it. The permanent remedy is cropping and renewal to approved procedures with post-weld NDT.
retrieval_cards.why: Offering doublers as a repair method without that qualification is a standard mark-loser and a genuine engineering error.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Who takes the thickness measurements, who witnesses them, and when must they be taken?
retrieval_cards.answer: By a company certified for the purpose — the Code carries a dedicated annex of procedures for certifying a company engaged in thickness measurement of hull structures — and witnessed by the attending surveyor. Paragraph 1.5 requires that in any survey the measurements in areas requiring close-up survey be taken simultaneously with the close-up survey.
retrieval_cards.why: The certification requirement and the simultaneity rule are two precise, checkable points that show the whole chain has been understood.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Give the route for the substantial corrosion question.
retrieval_cards.answer: 1 Define — both limbs. 2 The corrosion-allowance model and the extension trigger. 3 The assessment criteria. 4 Inspection techniques. 5 What the finding changes at the renewal survey. 6 Repair methods. 7 The society's role.
retrieval_cards.why: Seven sections in the printed order of the stem's four demands, so nothing the examiner asked for is left without a home.
