blocks.h: The distinction that most candidates get wrong

blocks.p: The due-diligence proviso names the Assured, Owners, Managers or Superintendents or any of their onshore management. It does not name the Master, Officers or Crew — whose negligence is an insured peril in the very same clause.

Read those two facts together and the commercial logic is clear. The policy accepts the risk of human error by the people operating the ship, because that is what the owner is insuring against. It does not accept the risk of the owner's own organisation failing to run the ship properly, because that would be insuring the owner against himself.

blocks.h: Common mistakes

ul: Citing the UK Marine Insurance Act 1906. The Indian statute is the Marine Insurance Act, 1963. This is a standing correction in this corpus and it is checked.
Treating perils of the sea as meaning 'anything that happens at sea'. It is a narrow term with two tests.
Forgetting that the loss must be fortuitous, and so listing wear and tear, corrosion or inherent vice among the covered perils.
Answering the second demand with only 'take out another policy' and missing the P&I club, which is how third-party liabilities are actually covered.
Getting the burden backwards and saying the assured must prove he exercised due diligence. He must prove the peril; the insurer must prove want of diligence.
Putting the Master and crew into the due-diligence list. Their negligence is the insured peril.
Saying latent defect cover pays for renewing the defective part. It pays for the resulting damage; the part itself is bought back by additional perils cover.
Quoting an Institute clause number. Several editions run concurrently and their numbering differs; enumerate the perils by substance.

blocks.h: Examiner traps

ul: 'Also enumerate' in the third sentence is a command for a list. Six items, named. A discursive paragraph on due diligence without the enumeration loses the marks the word 'enumerate' was protecting.
'Explain with examples' in the second sentence is likewise a command. Each route in section 3 must carry a concrete example.
The stem's phrase 'the onus of proof is upon the insurers' tells the candidate the answer to half the third demand. Restate it, justify it and use it — do not treat it as background.
The word barratry in the qualified group is a favourite oral follow-up, and it needs the phrase 'to the prejudice of the owner' to be defined correctly.
This is an Engineering Management paper, so the record-keeping consequences in section 6 are properly part of the answer, not an afterthought.

blocks.h: Likely oral follow-up

ul: Define perils of the seas. Is fire one?
Your main engine crankshaft breaks. Is that covered, and by which part of the policy?

Which Act governs your policy, and what does utmost good faith require of you?

blocks.h: Memory framework

blocks.p: NARROW, WIDER, OUTSIDE, QUALIFIED, WHO PROVES, WHAT IT MEANS ON BOARD. Six sections in the order the stem sets its demands, with section 2 inserted because the stem presupposes it.
For the qualified group, one line: BOILERS, SHAFTS, LATENT DEFECT, NEGLIGENCE, REPAIRERS, BARRATRY — and the proviso reaches the office, not the ship.

blocks.h: Uncertainty and jurisdiction notes

blocks.p: The corpus holds neither the statute nor the clauses. The Marine Insurance Act, 1963 is not held; the corpus carries a concept-level note supporting only sections 19, 20 and 66, and a subrogation section it marks 'VERIFY section'. Those limits are respected literally: no other section number is asserted anywhere in this answer, and the flagged section is not cited at all.

The statutory definition of perils of the seas lives in the Rules for Construction of Policy in the Schedule to the Act. The rule is stated as law because it is settled; its rule number is not asserted, because no held source fixes it and a wrong address is worse than none.

The Institute clause layer is industry documentation, and MIW's source-classification policy classifies the whole insurance area as citation and index only. No clause number and no edition is asserted, and the perils are enumerated by substance and grouping — which is also what an examiner wants, since several editions run concurrently in the market with different numbering.
No case authority is cited. The Inchmaree case is named only as the origin of the market's label for the clause, which is a matter of nomenclature rather than of precedent.

decomposition_gate.question_intent: A 16-mark undivided marine insurance question carrying three express demands and one implied one. Express: define and identify the perils of the sea that a marine policy covers; explain with examples what an insured can do about a peril that is not an insured peril; and enumerate the perils that are covered subject to a due-diligence proviso whose burden falls on the underwriters. Implied, and necessary to both later demands: that a hull policy covers a good deal that is NOT a peril of the sea, because the term itself is narrow.
decomposition_gate.mark_allocation: 16, undivided. The three printed demands suggest roughly 5 for the definition and its boundary, 4 for the routes to additional cover, and 7 for the qualified group and the burden - the last being the largest because the stem specifies it most precisely and because it is the only demand a weak candidate cannot bluff. Six sections weight it that way, with sections 4 and 5 together carrying the third demand.
decomposition_gate.examiner_expectation: The statutory definition - fortuitous accidents or casualties of the seas, excluding the ordinary action of wind and waves - with both tests drawn out and a list of what falls outside. The perils actually enumerated in a hull policy, with the recognition that most of them are not perils of the sea. Four routes to cover an uninsured peril, each with a concrete example, and the P&I route among them. Then the Inchmaree group named item by item, the due-diligence proviso stated with the persons it reaches, and the burden correctly allocated: the assured proves the peril, the insurer proves want of diligence. A strong answer states that the Master and crew are NOT in the diligence list, and closes on what that means for a Chief Engineer's records.

technical_ambiguities: 'Perils of the sea which are covered in a Marine Insurance contract' can be read as 'all perils covered' or as 'those perils that are properly perils of the sea'. The answer gives the narrow term first and then the full perils clause, which satisfies both readings and sets up the rest.

'A peril other than an insured peril of the sea' is ambiguous between a peril not covered at all and a maritime peril outside the perils-of-the-seas head. Both are answered: the routes in section 3 cover the first, and section 2 covers the second.

questions.understand_first: The whole question rests on one fact: 'perils of the sea' is a narrow legal term, not a description of everything that can go wrong on a voyage. It means fortuitous accidents or casualties of the seas — so the loss must be accidental rather than inevitable, and it must be caused by the sea rather than merely happening at sea. Fire proves the point: it is accidental, it happens at sea, and it is not a peril of the seas, which is why every policy lists it separately. Once that narrowness is seen, the rest of the question explains itself. The policy adds a list of other perils by express words because the first head is so narrow. Where even that list does not reach, the owner buys cover elsewhere — extension, separate policy, P&I entry, better terms. And for the machinery perils that the courts had held were not perils of the seas — a broken shaft, a burst boiler, a latent defect, an engineer's mistake — the market wrote the Inchmaree clause, and attached to it the one qualification that makes this an examinable question: the cover is lost if the loss resulted from want of due diligence by shore management, and it is the underwriters, not the owner, who must prove that it did.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Define 'perils of the seas' and give the two tests.
retrieval_cards.answer: Under the Rules for Construction of Policy in the Schedule to the Marine Insurance Act, 1963, the term refers only to fortuitous accidents or casualties of the seas and does not include the ordinary action of the winds and waves. Two tests: the loss must be fortuitous — accidental, not inevitable; and it must be of the sea, not merely at sea — the sea must be the cause.
retrieval_cards.why: The narrowness of the term is what generates every other part of the question.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Is fire on board a peril of the seas?
retrieval_cards.answer: No. It is accidental and it happens at sea, but the sea did not cause it, so it fails the second test. That is exactly why fire and explosion are listed separately in the perils clause of every hull policy.
retrieval_cards.why: The cleanest single proof of the definition, and it converts a memorised sentence into demonstrated understanding.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Enumerate the perils covered subject to a due-diligence proviso.
retrieval_cards.answer: The Inchmaree clause group: bursting of boilers; breakage of shafts; latent defect in the machinery or hull; negligence of Master, Officers, Crew or Pilots; negligence of repairers or charterers not assured under the policy; and barratry of Master, Officers or Crew. Covered provided the loss has not resulted from want of due diligence by the Assured, Owners, Managers or Superintendents or any of their onshore management.
retrieval_cards.why: The stem says 'enumerate'. Six named items are the marks; a paragraph about diligence is not.

retrieval_cards.prompt: In a broken-shaft claim, who must prove what?
retrieval_cards.answer: The assured proves that the loss was caused by a peril insured against — here, breakage of shafts. The due-diligence provision is a proviso limiting the insurer's liability, not a condition precedent, so the underwriters must prove want of due diligence by the owners, managers, superintendents or onshore management. The assured never has to prove that he was diligent.
retrieval_cards.why: This is the express point of the stem's third demand, and getting it backwards is the standard error.

retrieval_cards.prompt: The Second Engineer's mistake wrecked a bearing. The superintendent ignored a reported defect. Same answer?
retrieval_cards.answer: No. Negligence of the Master, Officers and Crew is an insured peril in the Inchmaree clause, so the engineer's mistake is covered. The due-diligence proviso names the Assured, Owners, Managers, Superintendents and onshore management — the crew are not in it. So the superintendent's failure to act on a reported defect is the fact that can defeat the claim.
retrieval_cards.why: The commercial logic is that a policy insures the owner against operational human error but not against his own organisation's failure to run the ship.

retrieval_cards.why: The stem says 'explain with examples', and the P&I route is the one candidates most often omit.

retrieval_cards.prompt: What is barratry, and why is it insured?
retrieval_cards.answer: A wrongful act wilfully committed by the Master, Officers or Crew to the prejudice of the owner — scuttling, wilful deviation, smuggling that leads to seizure. It is insured because from the owner's point of view it is a genuine fortuity, and by definition it is done without his privity.
retrieval_cards.why: A favourite oral follow-up, and the phrase 'to the prejudice of the owner' is what makes the definition correct.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Latent defect is found in a casting. Who pays for the new casting?
retrieval_cards.answer: Ordinarily the owner. Latent defect cover under the Inchmaree clause pays for the damage resulting from the defect, not for renewing the defective part itself. Buying back the cost of the part is precisely what an additional perils extension does, for extra premium.
retrieval_cards.why: A precise and commonly-missed limit on a cover candidates assume is complete.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Which Act governs an Indian marine policy, and what are the traps?
retrieval_cards.answer: The Marine Insurance Act, 1963 — section 19 utmost good faith, section 20 disclosure of every material circumstance known to the assured before the contract is concluded, section 66 general average loss. Not the UK Marine Insurance Act 1906, which is its model but not the operative statute, and the UK Insurance Act 2015 reform of the avoidance remedy does not apply to Indian law.
retrieval_cards.why: A standing correction in this corpus: coaching material routinely attributes the principles to the 1906 Act.

blocks.h: 1. The Convention, and its status at this sitting

blocks.p: The instrument is the International Convention on Liability and Compensation for Damage in Connection with the Carriage of Hazardous and Noxious Substances by Sea, 1996, as amended by the Protocol of 2010. Article 18 of the Protocol directs that the two instruments be read and interpreted together as one single instrument, and the resulting text is what is meant by 'the 2010 HNS Convention'.

Deal with the stem's premise first, because it is a statement about time and this is March 2025. The question asserts that the Convention 'is expected shortly to come into force'. At this sitting the Convention is not in force, and its entry-into-force conditions have not been met. The premise is preserved as the position the paper takes and the answer neither adopts it as a prediction nor contradicts the examiner: the correct statement is that the Convention has been adopted and is not yet in force.

That has a consequence worth stating in one line, because it is what makes the rest of the answer safe: the Convention's substantive provisions were fixed by the 2010 Protocol. Definitions, heads of damage, exclusions, limits and the certificate do not change while the instrument waits, so everything below can be stated with confidence even though nothing below is yet enforceable.

The scheme in one sentence: strict liability on the shipowner up to a limit, backed by compulsory insurance and a certificate, with a second tier funded by receivers of HNS cargo — the same two-tier architecture as the CLC and Fund regime, transplanted from oil to chemicals.

blocks.h: 2. (a) The substances covered - the seven categories of article 1.5

blocks.p: The Convention does not list commodities. Article 1.5(a) defines HNS as any substances, materials and articles carried on board a ship as cargo falling within seven categories, and each category is defined by reference to another IMO instrument. The effect is that the HNS list updates automatically as those instruments are amended — which is the single most intelligent point available in this limb.

ol: (i) Oils carried in bulk, as defined in regulation 1 of MARPOL Annex I. Examples: crude oil, fuel oil, heavy diesel oil, lubricating oil.

(ii) Noxious liquid substances carried in bulk, as defined in regulation 1.10 of MARPOL Annex II, together with substances provisionally categorised in pollution category X, Y or Z under regulation 6.3. Examples: vegetable oils, phosphoric acid.

(iii) Dangerous liquid substances carried in bulk listed in chapter 17 of the IBC Code, and products for which preliminary carriage conditions have been prescribed under paragraph 1.1.6. Examples: benzene, styrene monomer, methanol, sulphuric acid.

(iv) Dangerous, hazardous and harmful substances, materials and articles in packaged form covered by the IMDG Code. Examples: drummed and containerised chemicals, corrosives, explosives, flammable solids.
(v) Liquefied gases listed in chapter 19 of the IGC Code, and products prescribed under paragraph 1.1.6. Examples: LNG, LPG, ammonia, ethylene, vinyl chloride monomer.
(vi) Liquid substances carried in bulk with a flashpoint not exceeding 60°C, measured by closed-cup test. Examples: gasoline, naphtha and similar light products.

(vii) Solid bulk materials possessing chemical hazards covered by the IMSBC Code, to the extent that they are also subject to the IMDG Code in effect in 1996 when carried in packaged form. Examples: ammonium nitrate and ammonium nitrate based fertilizers, seed cake.

blocks.p: Article 1.5(b) extends the definition to residues from the previous carriage in bulk of categories (a)(i) to (iii) and (v) to (vii). A tank that has been discharged but not cleaned therefore still carries HNS for the purposes of the Convention — a point of real operational consequence.

blocks.h: 3. (a) Bulk HNS and packaged HNS - why the split matters

blocks.p: Article 1.5bis defines bulk HNS as categories (i) to (iii) and (v) to (vii) together with residues. Article 1.5ter defines packaged HNS as category (iv) alone.

The distinction is not academic. It fixes the owner's limit of liability under article 9 — a materially higher limit for packaged cargo — and in the second tier packaged cargo does not contribute to the Fund in the way bulk cargo does. It is also the reason a mixed or indeterminate cargo is treated under the packaged figures.

blocks.h: 4. (b) The heads of damage - article 1.6

blocks.p: The stem asks for 'types of pollution and subsequent losses or damages'. The Convention answers it directly: 'damage' under article 1.6 has four heads, and they are wider than pollution.

ol: Loss of life or personal injury, on board or outside the ship, caused by the substances. Note that this head has no pollution element at all — a fire, an explosion or a toxic release injuring people is squarely within it, and this is the largest single difference between HNS and the oil regime.
Loss of or damage to property outside the ship.

Loss or damage by contamination of the environment, subject to an express restriction: compensation for impairment of the environment, other than loss of profit from such impairment, is limited to the costs of reasonable measures of reinstatement actually undertaken or to be undertaken. So a fisherman's lost earnings are recoverable as economic loss, while the ecological damage itself is compensable only through the cost of reasonable restoration actually done or to be done.
The costs of preventive measures, and further loss or damage caused by preventive measures.

blocks.p: Article 1.6 also provides for the case where it is not reasonably possible to separate HNS damage from damage caused by other factors.

The four risks a candidate should name, because the stem says 'types of pollution': fire and explosion risk; toxicity to persons; contamination of sea, shore and air; and reactivity — and the Convention's own architecture reflects that the first two produce claims that no oil-pollution convention would reach.

blocks.h: 5. (b) What is excluded, and the mechanism that excludes it

blocks.p: Article 4 does the boundary work, and the mechanism is worth understanding because limb (c) depends on it.

ul: 4.1 — the Convention applies to claims other than those arising out of any contract for the carriage of goods and passengers. Cargo and passenger claims travel under their own regimes.
4.2 — it is disapplied where incompatible with workers' compensation or social security schemes.

4.3(a) — CLC pollution damage is excluded: 'pollution damage as defined in the International Convention on Civil Liability for Oil Pollution Damage, 1969, as amended, whether or not compensation is payable in respect of it under that Convention'. The italicised words are the mechanism: the exclusion bites on the definition, not on whether money is actually recoverable. There is no gap and no overlap by design.
4.3(b) — damage caused by radioactive material of class 7 in the IMDG Code or the IMSBC Code is excluded.
4.4 — warships and State ships on non-commercial service are excluded.

blocks.p: So the conventions are drafted to tile rather than to overlap: CLC takes persistent oil pollution damage, HNS takes the rest of the chemical risk including fire, explosion and toxic injury, and the Bunkers Convention takes bunker pollution that CLC does not already claim.

blocks.h: 6. (c) Why an oil products tanker needs certificates under all three

blocks.p: The answer is that the three conventions are defined by different things — one by the nature of the oil, one by the use of the oil, one by the category of the cargo — and a products tanker can satisfy all three definitions on the same voyage or on successive voyages.

CLC 1992. 'Oil' means any persistent hydrocarbon mineral oil, whether carried on board a ship as cargo or in the bunkers of such a ship (article I.5). A products tanker carrying a persistent product — fuel oil, heavy diesel, lubricating oil — is a CLC ship for that voyage, and article VII.1 requires a certificate where she carries more than 2,000 tons of oil in bulk as cargo. Note also article I.1: a combination carrier is a 'ship' only when actually carrying oil in bulk as cargo, and on a following voyage unless it is proved she retains no residues. Whether CLC applies therefore turns on two facts — is she a CLC ship, and is the oil persistent — and it must never be stated absolutely.

Bunkers Convention 2001. Bunker oil is any hydrocarbon mineral oil, including lubricating oil, used or intended to be used for the operation or propulsion of the ship, and any residues (article 1.5). A certificate is required of the registered owner of a ship of gross tonnage greater than 1000 (article 7.1). But article 4.1 disapplies the Convention to pollution damage as defined in the CLC, whether or not compensation is payable under it — so on a voyage when she is a CLC ship, a bunker spill is CLC damage, and the Bunkers certificate covers her on the voyages when she is not.

HNS. A products tanker frequently carries cargoes inside the seven categories that are not persistent oil: gasoline and naphtha fall in category (vi) as liquids in bulk with a flashpoint not exceeding 60°C; chemical and vegetable-oil parcels fall in (ii) or (iii). She then needs an HNS certificate under article 12, which applies to a ship registered in a State Party actually carrying HNS.

The reason all three are needed at once is commercial, and it is the point of the limb. A products tanker's trade is not one cargo. She loads gasoline this voyage, fuel oil the next and a chemical parcel the one after, and she carries bunkers throughout. Certificates are issued in advance and are checked in port; she cannot obtain one at the loading berth for the cargo she has just been fixed on. So she carries all three because which regime applies is decided by the cargo of the day, and residues under article 1.5(b) and CLC article I.1 mean the previous cargo can still reach her on the next voyage.

blocks.h: 7. (c) The certificate itself, and the two tiers behind it

blocks.p: Under article 12 the owner of a ship registered in a State Party and actually carrying HNS must maintain insurance or other financial security in the sums fixed by article 9.1, evidenced by a certificate in the Annex I model form, carried on board, mutually recognised between States Parties, and supporting direct action against the insurer under article 12.8. That structure is deliberately identical to the CLC and Bunkers certificates, which is why one officer can be expected to understand all three.
The limits that the certificate must cover, under article 9.1, and note that they differ by the bulk and packaged split from section 3:

ul: Bulk HNS — 10 million units of account for a ship not exceeding 2,000 units of tonnage, rising by 1,500 units per ton and then by 360 units per ton, capped at 100 million units of account.
Packaged HNS, or a mixed or indeterminate cargo — 11.5 million units of account, rising by 1,725 and then 414, capped at 115 million units of account.

blocks.p: The second tier. Where the owner's limit is insufficient, the HNS Fund, financed by contributions from receivers of HNS cargo in States Parties, pays the balance. Article 14.5(a) caps the whole scheme: the total of Fund compensation and any amount paid under chapter II shall not exceed 250 million units of account.

Liability and time. Article 7.1 imposes strict liability on the owner, with defences in 7.2(a) to (d) including the shipper's failure to furnish information on the hazardous nature of the substances, and article 7.5 channels claims away from crew, pilot, charterer, manager, operator and salvor. Article 37 extinguishes rights three years from the date the claimant knew or ought reasonably to have known of the damage, and in no case later than ten years from the incident.

blocks.h: Why this structure scores

blocks.p: Three printed limbs at 6, 5 and 5, and the marks are unusually easy to lose in limb (a) by trying to remember chemicals. The structure removes that risk by making the first point of limb (a) the mechanism: the Convention lists no commodities, it points at seven other IMO instruments. A candidate who says that and then names the seven instruments has the limb, and the examples are decoration on top of it.

Section 1 spends a paragraph on status because the stem makes a claim about time that a candidate must handle without contradicting the examiner. The right move is neither to repeat 'expected shortly' as fact nor to correct it, but to state the position precisely: adopted, not yet in force, entry-into-force conditions not met — and then to explain why the substance is nonetheless settled.

Crude, fuel oil, heavy diesel, lube oil
MARPOL Annex II reg 1.10; provisional X/Y/Z under 6.3
IBC Code ch.17; products under para 1.1.6

Flashpoint not exceeding 60 degrees C, closed cup, in bulk

blocks.p: Memorise the instruments, not the chemicals: Annex I, Annex II, IBC, IMDG, IGC, flashpoint, IMSBC. Category (iv) is the only packaged one, which is what article 1.5ter keys on.

blocks.h: The boundary between the three conventions

rows: PERSISTENT hydrocarbon mineral oil, as cargo or in the bunkers of such a ship
More than 2,000 tons of oil in bulk as cargo (art. VII.1)
Oil used or intended for the OPERATION OR PROPULSION of the ship, and residues - but disapplied where the damage is CLC pollution damage (art. 4.1)
CARGO within the seven categories of art. 1.5 - and CLC pollution damage is excluded by art. 4.3(a)
Ship registered in a State Party actually carrying HNS (art. 12)

blocks.p: The two exclusions — Bunkers article 4.1 and HNS article 4.3(a) — both bite on the CLC definition, and both say 'whether or not compensation is payable'. That phrase is the drafting device that makes the three regimes tile without gaps or overlaps, and quoting it is worth a mark on its own.

blocks.h: The standing correction on CLC

blocks.p: Never assert that CLC has no application to a bunker spill. CLC article I.5 covers persistent oil carried as cargo or in the bunkers of such a ship, and the Bunkers Convention excludes itself where the damage is CLC pollution damage. So a bunker spill from a CLC ship is CLC damage. Whether CLC applies turns on two facts and must be stated conditionally: is she a CLC ship, and is the oil persistent?

blocks.h: Common mistakes

ul: Trying to list chemicals in limb (a) instead of naming the seven referenced instruments.
Saying the Convention is in force, or predicting when it will be. It is adopted and not in force, and no date should be offered.
Quoting a number of Contracting States. No held source fixes it and none of the three limbs needs it.
Treating HNS as an oil-pollution convention. Its first head of damage is death and personal injury, with no pollution element at all.
Forgetting article 1.5(b) residues — a discharged but uncleaned tank still carries HNS.
Missing the bulk / packaged split, which changes the owner's limit and the Fund contribution.

Stating that environmental damage is fully compensable. Compensation for impairment of the environment, other than loss of profit, is limited to the cost of reasonable reinstatement measures actually undertaken or to be undertaken.
Saying CLC does not apply to bunkers. It does, where she is a CLC ship and the oil is persistent.
Converting units of account into dollars. They are Special Drawing Rights and the rate moves daily.

blocks.h: Examiner traps

ul: The stem's opening sentence, 'is expected shortly to come into force', is a premise you must handle rather than adopt or attack. State the position; do not predict.
'Types of pollution AND SUBSEQUENT LOSSES OR DAMAGES' is asking for the heads of damage under article 1.6, not for a description of chemical spills. Answer the legal question.

'Probably require' in limb (c) is doing real work. The examiner knows it depends on the cargo of the day, and the mark is for explaining why the trade makes all three likely, not for asserting that all three always apply.
'All 3 conventions' invites a comparison table. What earns the marks is the mechanism — three different defining criteria, and two exclusions that both bite on the CLC definition.
The Convention's own name is a mouthful, and getting '1996 as amended by the 2010 Protocol' right, with the single-instrument direction in Protocol article 18, is a cheap and visible mark.

blocks.h: Likely oral follow-up

ul: Is the HNS Convention in force? What are you waiting for?
Name the seven categories by the instrument each points at.
Your tank is discharged but not cleaned. Are you carrying HNS?
A cargo fire injures a stevedore. Is that within the Convention?
Who pays above the owner's limit, and what is the overall cap?
You are a products tanker with fuel oil aboard and a bunker spill. Which convention?
Same ship, gasoline cargo, bunker spill. Now which?
What is a unit of account?
How long does a claimant have?

blocks.h: Memory framework

blocks.p: STATUS, SUBSTANCES, SPLIT, DAMAGE, EXCLUSIONS, THREE CERTIFICATES, THE CERTIFICATE ITSELF. Seven sections, and the first two carry limb (a).
For the categories: Annex I, Annex II, IBC, IMDG, IGC, flashpoint, IMSBC — seven instruments, and only IMDG is packaged.
For limb (c), one line: CLC is about the oil's nature, Bunkers is about the oil's use, HNS is about the cargo's category — and a products tanker changes cargo every voyage.

questions.understand_first: The HNS Convention is the chemical equivalent of the CLC and Fund regime: strict liability on the owner up to a limit, compulsory insurance evidenced by a certificate, and a second tier funded by the receivers of the cargo. Two features make it different and both are examinable. First, it does not list chemicals — article 1.5 defines its scope by pointing at seven other IMO instruments, so the list of covered substances updates itself whenever those instruments are amended. Second, its damage is wider than pollution: the first head is death and personal injury, because a chemical cargo kills by fire, explosion and toxicity as well as by contamination, and no oil convention reaches that. The third limb is about boundaries. CLC is defined by the oil being persistent; Bunkers by the oil being used for the ship's operation or propulsion; HNS by the cargo's category. Both Bunkers and HNS then carve out anything the CLC definition already claims, using the same phrase — 'whether or not compensation is payable' — so the three tile rather than overlap. A products tanker carries gasoline this voyage, fuel oil the next and bunkers throughout, so she needs all three certificates because which regime applies is decided by the cargo of the day, and certificates cannot be obtained at the loading berth.

quick_revision.critical_regulation: HNS article 1.5 read with article 4.3(a). Article 1.5 defines the Convention's scope by reference to seven other IMO instruments rather than by listing commodities; article 4.3(a) excludes CLC pollution damage whether or not compensation is payable in respect of it under that Convention, which is the drafting device that makes CLC, Bunkers and HNS tile without gap or overlap.
quick_revision.major_trap: Treating HNS as an oil-pollution convention and answering limb (b) with a description of chemical spills. Its first head of damage is death and personal injury with no pollution element at all — fire, explosion and toxicity — and that is the largest single difference from the CLC regime. The second trap is saying the Convention is in force, or predicting when it will be. The third is asserting that CLC has no application to a bunker spill: CLC covers persistent oil whether carried as cargo or in the bunkers of such a ship, so a bunker spill from a CLC ship is CLC damage.

retrieval_cards.prompt: How does the HNS Convention define the substances it covers?
retrieval_cards.answer: Not by listing commodities. Article 1.5(a) covers any substances, materials and articles carried on board as cargo falling within seven categories, each defined by reference to another IMO instrument: MARPOL Annex I, MARPOL Annex II, the IBC Code, the IMDG Code, the IGC Code, a flashpoint test not exceeding 60°C, and the IMSBC Code. Article 1.5(b) adds residues from previous bulk carriage.
retrieval_cards.why: The mechanism is worth more than any list of chemicals, and it is what makes the scope self-updating.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Give the four heads of damage under article 1.6.
retrieval_cards.answer: (a) Loss of life or personal injury, on board or outside the ship, caused by the substances. (b) Loss of or damage to property outside the ship. (c) Loss or damage by contamination of the environment — but compensation for impairment other than loss of profit is limited to the costs of reasonable measures of reinstatement actually undertaken or to be undertaken. (d) The costs of preventive measures and further loss caused by them.
retrieval_cards.why: Head (a) requires no pollution at all, which is the point most candidates miss about this Convention.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Is the HNS Convention in force?
retrieval_cards.answer: No. It is adopted and not in force, and its entry-into-force conditions are not met. Do not offer a date and do not quote a number of Contracting States. Its substantive provisions were nonetheless fixed by the 2010 Protocol, so definitions, damage heads, exclusions, limits and the certificate can all be stated with confidence.
retrieval_cards.why: The stem asserts it is 'expected shortly to come into force'. The correct handling is to state the position without contradicting the examiner and without predicting.

retrieval_cards.prompt: What defines each of CLC, Bunkers and HNS?
retrieval_cards.answer: CLC 1992 — the oil's nature: persistent hydrocarbon mineral oil, as cargo or in the bunkers of such a ship. Bunkers 2001 — the oil's use: oil used or intended for the operation or propulsion of the ship, plus residues. HNS — the cargo's category under article 1.5. Both Bunkers (art. 4.1) and HNS (art. 4.3(a)) then carve out anything within the CLC definition, whether or not compensation is payable.
retrieval_cards.why: Three different defining criteria plus two identical carve-outs is the whole of limb (c) in four lines.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Does CLC apply to a bunker spill?
retrieval_cards.answer: It can, and it must never be answered absolutely. CLC article I.5 covers persistent oil carried as cargo or in the bunkers of such a ship, and Bunkers article 4.1 excludes itself where the damage is CLC pollution damage. So a bunker spill from a CLC ship is CLC damage. It turns on two facts: is she a CLC ship, and is the oil persistent?
retrieval_cards.why: A standing correction in this corpus, and the reason a products tanker's answer depends on the cargo of the day.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Why does a products tanker carry all three certificates?
retrieval_cards.answer: Because her trade is not one cargo. Gasoline or naphtha this voyage falls in HNS category (vi); fuel oil next voyage makes her a CLC ship; bunkers are aboard throughout. Certificates are issued in advance and inspected in port, so she cannot obtain one at the loading berth for the cargo she has just been fixed on — and residues under HNS 1.5(b) and CLC article I.1 mean the previous cargo can still reach her on the next voyage.
retrieval_cards.why: The stem says 'probably require', and explaining the dependency is what earns the mark.

retrieval_cards.prompt: State the HNS limits and the overall cap.
retrieval_cards.answer: Article 9.1(a) bulk: 10 million units of account up to 2,000 units of tonnage, rising by 1,500 then 360 per ton, capped at 100 million. Article 9.1(b) packaged, mixed or indeterminate: 11.5 million, rising by 1,725 then 414, capped at 115 million. Article 14.5(a): the total of Fund compensation and any amount paid under chapter II must not exceed 250 million units of account. Units of account are SDRs.
retrieval_cards.why: The bulk/packaged split is why the two-limit structure exists, and the 250 million cap is the ceiling of the whole scheme.

retrieval_cards.prompt: What does the article 12 certificate require, and how long does a claimant have?
retrieval_cards.answer: Article 12: the owner of a ship registered in a State Party and actually carrying HNS must maintain insurance or other financial security in the article 9.1 sums, evidenced by a certificate in the Annex I model form, carried on board, mutually recognised between States Parties, with direct action against the insurer under 12.8. Article 37: rights extinguish three years from knowledge of the damage, and in no case later than ten years from the incident.
retrieval_cards.why: The certificate structure is deliberately identical to CLC and Bunkers, which is why one officer can understand all three.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Bulk HNS or packaged HNS - which is which, and why does it matter?
retrieval_cards.answer: Article 1.5bis: bulk HNS is categories (i) to (iii) and (v) to (vii), plus residues. Article 1.5ter: packaged HNS is category (iv) alone — the IMDG Code category. It matters because it sets the owner's limit of liability under article 9, packaged cargo does not contribute to the Fund as bulk cargo does, and a mixed or indeterminate cargo takes the packaged figures.
retrieval_cards.why: The split is the bridge between limb (a) and the limits in limb (c).

The canonical record for regulation 24 was read directly this session and it carries the finding that governs this whole question: TABLE 1 PRINTS TWO DIFFERENT PHASE TIMETABLES, and the split is by ship type. Gas carriers of 15,000 DWT and above, all containerships, general cargo ships, LNG carriers and cruise passenger ships ran Phase 2 from 1 January 2020 to 31 MARCH 2022 and entered Phase 3 on 1 APRIL 2022; bulk carriers, the smaller gas-carrier bands, tankers, refrigerated cargo carriers, combination carriers and all ro-ro classes ran Phase 2 from 1 January 2020 to 31 DECEMBER 2024 and entered Phase 3 on 1 JANUARY 2025. blocks.h: 1. Where the duty comes from, and the numbering that matters

blocks.p: The EEDI lives in chapter 4 of MARPOL Annex VI, as revised by resolution MEPC.328(76), which entered into force on 1 November 2022. Use the post-2021 numbering; the older scheme still circulates in notes and is wrong.

ul: Regulation 19 — application: chapter 4 applies to ships of 400 gross tonnage and above, and regulation 19.3 disapplies regulations 22 to 25 to ships with non-conventional propulsion.

Regulation 22 — the attained EEDI: calculated for each new ship, ship-specific, recorded in an EEDI technical file, and verified by the Administration or an authorized organization. Regulation 22.2 refers the calculation method out to guidelines adopted by the Organization.
Regulation 24 — the required EEDI, and this is where the phased scheme lives.
Regulation 5.4 — the initial survey verifying the attained EEDI; regulation 6 — the International Energy Efficiency Certificate.

blocks.p: Regulation 24.1 states the duty in one line: for each new ship, the attained EEDI shall be less than or equal to the required EEDI, where
required EEDI = (1 − X/100) × reference line value
X is the reduction factor taken from Table 1 for the ship's type, size band and phase, and the reference line value comes from Table 2's parameters against the ship's deadweight or gross tonnage.

blocks.h: 2. What 'Phase 2' means at this sitting - and the answer is not what the stem assumes

blocks.p: The stem asks about the present EEDI framework under Phase 2. That premise needs handling precisely, and doing so is worth marks rather than costing them.
Table 1 prints two different phase timetables, and the split is by ship type.

rows: Gas carriers of 15,000 DWT and above; all containerships; general cargo ships; LNG carriers; cruise passenger ships
Bulk carriers; the smaller gas-carrier bands; tankers; refrigerated cargo carriers; combination carriers; all ro-ro classes

blocks.p: It follows that at this sitting Phase 2 has closed on both timetables — on the first nearly three years ago, and on the second only ten weeks before this paper. The present phase for a ship contracted today is Phase 3, whichever timetable she is on.
Three further points of precision, and each is a mark.

ol: Phase 2 is nonetheless still operative law, and the stem is not wrong to ask about it. A ship's required EEDI is fixed by the phase she was contracted or built into, so an expired phase continues to govern a large part of the existing fleet for the rest of its life. Phase 0 and Phase 1 are the same.

The phase a ship falls in is fixed by her construction datum, and regulation 24 does not print the datum rule. 'New ship' is regulation 2.2.18 — contract on or after 1 January 2013, or keel laid on or after 1 July 2013, or delivery on or after 1 July 2015. For a converted ship, regulation 5.4 requires the phase to be determined for the original ship under 2.2.18, while regulation 24.2 supplies only the conversion-date datum for ship type and size. Three datum rules in three regulations.

The stem's bracket '20% – 30%' spans two phases. The reduction factors recurring across Table 1 are 0, 10, 20 and 30; 20 per cent is characteristically the Phase 2 figure for the larger bands and 30 per cent the Phase 3 figure. The bracket therefore describes the stringency band the question is aiming at, and the design features that meet it are the same either way — which is why the rest of this answer is unaffected.

blocks.p: Note also that none of Table 1's dates is an amendment or entry-into-force date. They are phase boundaries printed in the enacted text, and regulation 24 is itself unamended.

blocks.h: 3. The equation - because every design feature attacks one side of it

blocks.p: The attained EEDI is, in structure, grammes of CO2 emitted per tonne-mile of transport work:
attained EEDI ≈ (engine power × specific fuel consumption × carbon factor) ÷ (capacity × reference speed)

with correction factors for ice class, technical and regulatory power limits, cubic capacity, weather, voluntary structural enhancement and innovative energy efficiency technologies. The full method is referred out by regulation 22.2 to Organization guidelines, so a candidate should give the structure and not attempt the coefficients.
Every design measure therefore does one of four things, and organising the answer by mechanism rather than by a list of gadgets is what earns a first-class mark:

ol: Reduce the power needed for a given speed — sections 4 and 6.
Reduce the carbon factor of the fuel — section 5. The largest single lever.
Reduce fuel consumed per unit of power, or recover energy already paid for — section 6.
Raise the denominator — more capacity, or a reference speed the design can actually sustain — section 7.

blocks.h: 4. Design features that reduce required power - hull and propulsion

blocks.p: This is where a new build has freedom that no retrofit has, and it should be written first.

ol: Hull form optimisation for the real operating profile. Computational fluid dynamics and model testing against the speed and draught the ship will actually trade at, rather than a single contract condition. Slender entrance, optimised aft body and buttock flow, reduced wetted surface.
Bulbous bow designed for the operating envelope, not for one condition. Over-designed bulbs at part load are a known cause of poor real-world performance.

Reduced installed power and a lower design speed. Because the numerator carries engine power directly and resistance rises far faster than speed, a modest reduction in design speed is the most powerful single design decision available. New builds have been designed slower for exactly this reason.

A larger, slower-turning propeller with a bigger diameter and lower revolutions, matched to an aperture designed for it. Propulsive efficiency rises with diameter; the constraint is draught and clearance, and on a new build both are design variables.
High-efficiency propeller design — optimised blade area, pitch distribution, skew and section, with the wake field from the hull optimisation used as the design input rather than assumed.
Optimised hull and propeller interaction: shaft line arrangement, stern tube alignment, twin-skeg or single-skeg selection, and rudder profile chosen with the propeller rather than after it.
Low-friction and foul-release coatings specified from new, so that the ship enters service on her design resistance.

Engine selection and tuning: derated, long-stroke, low-revolution main engines matched to the larger propeller, with electronic control giving low specific fuel consumption across the load range rather than at one point.

Reduced auxiliary demand: variable-frequency drives on pumps and fans, correctly sized rather than over-sized auxiliaries, efficient HVAC and lighting, and demand-based control. Auxiliary power appears in the numerator too and is routinely neglected in answers.

blocks.h: 5. Design features that reduce the carbon factor - the fuel

blocks.p: The carbon conversion factor sits in the numerator as a straight multiplier, so a fuel with less carbon per unit of energy reduces the attained EEDI directly and by more than any hull measure. On a new build the choice is genuinely open.

ul: LNG dual-fuel, using low-pressure or high-pressure gas injection. The largest single EEDI reduction available from an otherwise conventional design, and the reason so many Phase 2 and Phase 3 compliant designs are gas-fuelled.
LPG, particularly on gas carriers where the cargo is the fuel.
Methanol dual-fuel, with the advantage of a liquid fuel at ambient conditions and much simpler containment.
Ammonia and hydrogen capability, or ammonia-ready and methanol-ready designs where the space, tank foundations and safety arrangements are built in for later conversion.
Biofuel capability in the fuel system and materials specification.

blocks.p: Two qualifications should be stated, because an unqualified fuel answer is not a Class I answer. First, gas fuelling introduces methane slip, which is a greenhouse gas the EEDI's carbon factor does not fully capture, so the index gain overstates the climate gain. Second, the index is a tank-to-wake, design-condition measure and says nothing about how the fuel was produced.

blocks.h: 6. Design features that recover or displace energy

ol: Waste heat recovery. Exhaust gas economiser with a steam turbine, an exhaust power turbine, or a combined turbo-generator feeding the ship's electrical load and, through a shaft motor, the propulsion. The most substantial single item of machinery-side design available.
Shaft generator, taking the electrical load from the more efficient main engine and removing auxiliary engine running at sea; and a shaft motor for power take-in.

Energy saving devices around the propeller, which recover rotational and hub losses: pre-swirl ducts and stators, wake-equalising ducts, propeller boss cap fins, rudder bulbs and twisted rudders. On a new build these are designed with the hull and propeller rather than bolted on, which is why they perform better on a newbuilding than as a retrofit.
Air lubrication — a bubble or air-cavity layer reducing frictional resistance, with the compressor power correctly debited against the gain.
Wind assistance — rotor sails, rigid wing sails, suction wings or kites, integrated with deck arrangement and visibility lines from the design stage.
Solar contribution to hotel load, which is small but admissible.
Battery hybridisation for peak shaving and for load levelling of the auxiliary plant.

blocks.p: Several of these enter the calculation through the innovative energy efficiency technology terms of the formula, which is how the regulation credits a technology that does not simply reduce shaft power.

blocks.h: 7. Raising the denominator - and the floor that stops power being cut

blocks.p: The denominator is capacity multiplied by reference speed, so a design that carries more per unit of installed power scores better.

ul: Increased deadweight or cubic capacity for the same principal dimensions — lighter structure through high-tensile steel and optimised scantlings, improved hull volume utilisation, and reduced lightship.
Beamier, shallower forms at lower speed, which raise capacity and reduce required power together.
Design draught and trim optimisation, so that the reference condition and the trading condition are the same ship.

blocks.p: And the limit. Regulation 24.5 carries a minimum propulsion power requirement. It exists because the cheapest way to pass the index is to install less power, and a ship with too little power cannot keep steerage and manoeuvre in adverse conditions — which is a safety matter, and a real one after several underpowered designs. The numerical criteria live in Organization guidelines. Regulation 24.6 carries the review trigger for the phase scheme itself.

This is the paragraph that distinguishes an engineer's answer: the EEDI is a design index, and it can be satisfied by making the ship worse. Regulation 24.5 is the regulation's own acknowledgement of that, and it is the reason the design features above are the legitimate route and power starvation is not.

blocks.h: 8. How the result is verified and certified

blocks.p: Design features only count if they survive verification, and the stem's word 'comply' reaches this.

ol: The shipbuilder calculates the attained EEDI and compiles the EEDI technical file — principal particulars, capacity, rated power, specific fuel consumption from the NOx Technical File, and every correction factor claimed.
Preliminary verification at the design stage, against the technical file and the approved drawings.

Final verification at the sea trial, where the reference speed is established from the measured speed-power relationship corrected to the reference condition. This is the only quantity in the whole index that cannot be known on paper, which is why verification is in two stages.
The Administration or an authorized organization verifies the attained EEDI — it does not calculate it and does not approve it.
The result is recorded and the International Energy Efficiency Certificate issued under regulation 6, following the initial survey under regulation 5.4.
Claims for innovative technologies must be substantiated in the technical file; a device fitted but not evidenced earns nothing in the index.

blocks.h: Why this structure scores

blocks.p: Sixteen marks, undivided, on a question that invites a shapeless list of fuel-saving gadgets. The structure defeats that by putting the equation at section 3 and then organising every design feature by which part of the equation it attacks. A candidate who writes 'these measures reduce the numerator, these reduce the carbon factor, these raise the denominator' has produced an engineering argument rather than a catalogue, and the marks follow.

Section 2 exists because the stem contains a claim about time that is false at this sitting, and handling it correctly is worth marks. Section 7 exists because the honest engineering answer to 'how do I pass this index' includes 'by installing less power', and the regulation itself had to legislate against that.

blocks.h: The phase position at this sitting — the single most valuable fact

rows: Gas carriers 15,000 DWT and above; containerships; general cargo ships; LNG carriers; cruise passenger ships
Bulk carriers; smaller gas-carrier bands; tankers; reefers; combination carriers; all ro-ro classes

blocks.p: Both timetables have moved past Phase 2 by March 2025, the second by only ten weeks. Two things follow that a candidate must hold together. The stem's word 'present' is out of date — but Phase 2 remains operative law, because a ship's required EEDI is fixed by the phase she was contracted or built into, and an expired phase governs its cohort for life.
Applying one timetable to the other's ships is the classic error here: it shifts a 30 per cent obligation by two years and nine months.

blocks.h: Three datum rules in three regulations

ul: Regulation 2.2.18 — what makes her a 'new ship': contract on or after 1 January 2013, keel on or after 1 July 2013, or delivery on or after 1 July 2015.
Regulation 5.4 — for a converted ship, the phase is determined for the original ship under 2.2.18.
Regulation 24.2 — supplies only the conversion-date datum for ship type and size.

blocks.p: Regulation 24 itself does not print the datum rule, which is why a candidate who reads only Table 1 cannot say which phase a given ship is in.

blocks.h: Do not confuse EEDI with EEXI

rows: PHASED - four dated phases, two timetables
NOT phased - a single fixed factor per type and size band
Genuine design - hull, propeller, fuel, energy recovery
Two stages - preliminary at design, final at sea trial

blocks.p: The phase language attaches itself to EEXI in conversation because the EEXI factors were derived from the EEDI reference lines. Here the phases are genuinely the subject, and power limitation is not an answer: the required EEDI is set against the ship's own design, so a limited-power ship simply is a lower-powered design.

blocks.h: Common mistakes

ul: Using the pre-2021 numbering. Regulation 21 is functional requirements, not the required EEDI. The revised Annex renumbered chapter 4 when it entered into force on 1 November 2022.
Writing a list of devices with no reference to the equation, so that the answer cannot explain why any of them helps.
Omitting the fuel, which is the single largest lever available to a new build.
Claiming LNG is a decarbonisation answer without mentioning methane slip.
Quoting a reduction factor for a named ship type from memory. Table 1 has 123 such cells across 27 size bands and four phases, and the wrong cell is worse than no cell.
Quoting percentage gains for energy-saving devices. They are ship-specific and mostly come from maker's material.
Ignoring auxiliary power, which is in the numerator.
Missing regulation 24.5, the minimum propulsion power floor, which is the regulation's own answer to the obvious loophole.
Treating EEDI as measured performance. It is a design index calculated at a reference condition; only the reference speed comes from trials.
Importing the IMO Net-Zero Framework, which was approved in April 2025 — the month after this sitting.

blocks.h: Examiner traps

ul: 'The present EEDI framework under Phase 2' is the trap. Phase 2 had closed on both timetables by this sitting. Answer the question fully, state the position precisely, and do not lecture the examiner.
'(of 20% -30% reduction)' spans two phases. The recurring Table 1 values are 0, 10, 20 and 30. Treat the bracket as naming a stringency band, not a single factor.
The stem prints 'EEDl' with a lower-case L. It is a printing artefact; do not reproduce it and do not remark on it.

'Design features' is the operative phrase. Operational measures — slow steaming, trim optimisation in service, hull cleaning — belong to the SEEMP and the CII and do not affect the attained EEDI. Including them without saying so is a mark lost.
'For new builds in 2013' is the stem's own date for the introduction of the requirement, and it matches Phase 0 beginning 1 January 2013. It is correct and needs no comment.

blocks.h: Memory framework

blocks.p: One equation and four attacks. CO2 over transport work (3) — then LESS POWER (4), LESS CARBON (5), RECOVER ENERGY (6), MORE CARGO (7), with VERIFY (8) at the end and the phase position (2) at the front.
For the phases: containerships and gas went to Phase 3 in April 2022; bulkers and tankers in January 2025. Two dates, and the second is ten weeks before this paper.

blocks.h: Uncertainty and currency

blocks.p: The corpus's MARPOL Annex VI is frozen and citation-ready, and its export policy is facts and pointers only: identity, structure, duty-bearers and numerics are usable and no body text is reproduced. This answer observes that policy throughout.

No reduction factor and no reference-line coefficient is quoted. Table 1 carries 123 reduction-factor cells across 27 size bands and four phases, and Table 2 carries 32 parameters; every cell governs a distinct ship type, size band and phase, so a value quoted for the wrong band or phase is actively wrong. The method is given and the numbers are not.

The calculation method is referred out by regulation 22.2 to Organization guidelines the corpus does not hold and which were not read, so the formula's structure is authoritative secondary and no correction factor, default consumption or carbon factor is quoted as a number. The same applies to the numerical criteria for the minimum propulsion power requirement under regulation 24.5, which the corpus records as quantitative in subject while printing no quantity.
No efficiency percentage is claimed for any energy-saving device. Those figures are ship-specific, condition-dependent and largely originate in maker's material.

decomposition_gate.question_intent: A single 16-mark design question with a false premise printed into it. The examinable content is the set of DESIGN features by which a new build meets a required EEDI, and it is testing whether the candidate can organise them by mechanism rather than recite them. The premise - that Phase 2 is the present framework - is out of date at this sitting, and handling that correctly is a second, smaller demand the strong candidate will meet.
decomposition_gate.mark_allocation: 16, undivided, and the stem's own emphasis is on 'the various design features'. Sections 4 to 7 therefore carry the bulk. Sections 1, 2 and 3 are framing and are kept tight - but section 2 cannot be cut, because the phase position is the paper's sharpest temporal point, and section 3 cannot be cut, because without the equation the design features are a list.
decomposition_gate.examiner_expectation: The correct post-2021 regulation numbering - 22 attained, 24 required, Table 1 - and the required EEDI formula. Then design features grouped so that their effect is explained: hull form and operating-profile optimisation, reduced installed power and design speed, larger slower propeller and matched engine, coatings, auxiliary demand; the fuel, which is the largest single lever, with methane slip acknowledged; waste heat recovery, shaft generator, propeller-zone energy-saving devices, air lubrication and wind assistance; and capacity measures. A strong answer also reaches the minimum propulsion power floor in regulation 24.5 and the two-stage verification.
primary_source_plan: Read the corpus's frozen canonical record for regulation 24 at source, because Table 1's phase structure is the temporal heart of the question and cannot be recalled safely.
Establish from that record BOTH phase timetables and their split by ship type, and confirm where each phase stands at March 2025 rather than assuming Phase 2 is current because the stem says so.

Carry the regulation identities and the verification architecture from QP2502-Q6, the immediately preceding sitting, whose temporal record establishes that regulation 22 is unamended and that MEPC.385(81) touches no EEDI regulation - and re-check that finding for March 2025 rather than inheriting it.
Read QP2410-Q8's printed stem and donor analysis, to establish the limb-level relationship and to identify which of its findings INVERT rather than transfer.
Confirm the corpus export policy - facts and pointers only - before writing, so that no body text is reproduced and no Table 1 cell is quoted.
Confirm the Net-Zero Framework's approval date relative to this sitting and exclude it.
decomposition_gate.freshness_risk: HIGH, and concentrated in one place. The regulation is unamended and the engineering is stable, but the PHASE POSITION moved on 1 January 2025 - ten weeks before this sitting - for tankers, bulk carriers, reefers, combination carriers and ro-ro ships. Any answer written from a pre-2025 source states the phase position wrongly.
decomposition_gate.jurisdiction_risk: LOW. MARPOL Annex VI is international and operates through the flag Administration and its authorized organization. No Indian limb is set.
technical_ambiguities: 'The present EEDI framework under Phase 2' is false at this sitting on both timetables. Preserved and adjudicated: the design content is delivered in full and the position is stated precisely.

'(of 20% -30% reduction)' spans two phases. The recurring Table 1 values are 0, 10, 20 and 30, with 20 characteristically Phase 2 for the larger bands and 30 Phase 3. Treated as a stringency band rather than a single factor, and no cell is quoted.

'Design features adopted in the new build vessels to comply' excludes operational measures. Slow steaming in service, in-service trim optimisation and hull cleaning belong to the SEEMP and the CII and do not affect the attained EEDI. The distinction is stated rather than assumed.
The stem prints 'EEDl' with a lower-case L. A printing artefact; preserved in text_verbatim, not reproduced in the answer.

Reduced design speed is both a design feature and, in appearance, an operational one. It is a design feature here because the reference speed is a design parameter fixed at the trial, and that is worth saying.
decomposition_gate.target_answer_shape: Eight numbered sections. Three framing - the regulations with correct numbering and the formula; the phase position at this sitting with both timetables and the datum rules; and the equation with the four mechanisms it exposes. Then four sections of design features, one per mechanism - reduce power, reduce carbon, recover energy, raise capacity - with the minimum propulsion power floor closing the fourth. Then verification and certification, because the stem's word is 'comply'.

reverify_before_publication.why: The calculation method is REFERRED OUT by regulation 22.2 to Organization guidelines which the corpus does not hold and which were not read. The structure is stated as authoritative secondary and NO coefficient, default specific fuel consumption or carbon conversion factor is quoted as a number.

reverify_before_publication.why: The corpus record states that regulation 24.5 is quantitative in subject while printing no quantity, its numerical criteria living in Organization guidelines that are not held. The floor is described by function and purpose; no figure is asserted.

reverify_before_publication.claim: The design features and their effect on the index - hull optimisation, reduced power and speed, propeller and engine matching, fuels, energy recovery, energy-saving devices and capacity measures
reverify_before_publication.why: Established naval architecture and marine engineering, and industry design practice. No percentage efficiency gain is claimed for any device, because such figures are ship-specific, condition-dependent and largely originate in maker's material.

questions.understand_first: The EEDI is a design index, not a performance measurement: grammes of CO2 per tonne-mile that the ship's design will produce at a reference condition. Regulation 24.1 says the attained EEDI must be less than or equal to the required EEDI, which is (1 − X/100) of a reference line for her type and size — and X tightens by phase. So every design feature in this answer is an attack on one side of a single fraction: CO2 over transport work. Reduce the power needed, reduce the carbon in the fuel, recover energy you have already paid for, or carry more cargo. Organise the answer that way and it explains itself; list gadgets and it does not. Two further things a Class I candidate should hold. The stem says 'the present ... Phase 2', and at this March 2025 sitting that is out of date on both of Table 1's timetables — containerships and gas carriers moved to Phase 3 in April 2022, and tankers, bulk carriers and ro-ros on 1 January 2025, ten weeks before this paper. And the cheapest way to pass this index is to install less power, which is why regulation 24.5 had to legislate a minimum propulsion power floor. Naming that shows you understand what the index actually measures.

questions.memory_cue: One fraction and four attacks — LESS POWER (4), LESS CARBON (5), RECOVER (6), MORE CARGO (7), then VERIFY (8). Front it with the phase position (2): containerships and gas went to Phase 3 in April 2022, tankers and bulkers on 1 January 2025.

quick_revision.recall_15s: MARPOL Annex VI ch.4, MEPC.328(76), in force 1 Nov 2022. Regulation 22 attained EEDI and the technical file; regulation 24 required EEDI = (1 − X/100) × reference line, X from Table 1 by type, size band and phase. Table 1 has TWO timetables: Phase 3 from 1 April 2022 for containerships, gas carriers 15,000 DWT and above, general cargo, LNG and cruise; from 1 January 2025 for bulkers, tankers, reefers, combination carriers and ro-ro. Phase 2 is closed on both by March 2025. Design = less power, less carbon, recover energy, more cargo. Floor: regulation 24.5 minimum propulsion power. Verified in two stages, certificate under regulation 6. Fuel is the largest lever — but LNG carries methane slip and ammonia is not a zero-emission fuel: no carbon in the molecule means no direct CO2, not zero emissions, because N2O and ammonia slip are emissions and the lifecycle depends on the production pathway.
critical_numbers: Required EEDI = (1 - X/100) x reference line value - regulation 24.1
Phase 2: 1 Jan 2020 to 31 MARCH 2022 for gas carriers 15,000 DWT+, containerships, general cargo, LNG, cruise - Phase 3 from 1 APRIL 2022
Phase 2: 1 Jan 2020 to 31 DECEMBER 2024 for bulk carriers, smaller gas bands, tankers, reefers, combination carriers, all ro-ro - Phase 3 from 1 JANUARY 2025
Phase 0: 1 Jan 2013 to 31 Dec 2014. Phase 1: 1 Jan 2015 to 31 Dec 2019 (1 Sep 2015 for six ship types)
Recurring Table 1 reduction factors: 0, 10, 20 and 30 - NO individual cell is quoted here
New ship, regulation 2.2.18: contract on/after 1 Jan 2013, keel on/after 1 Jul 2013, or delivery on/after 1 Jul 2015
Chapter 4 applies at 400 GT and above (regulation 19)
quick_revision.critical_regulation: MARPOL Annex VI regulation 24 read with regulation 22. Regulation 22 creates the attained EEDI, requires it to be ship-specific and recorded in an EEDI technical file, and refers the calculation method out to Organization guidelines; regulation 24.1 requires the attained EEDI to be less than or equal to (1 − X/100) × the reference line value, with X taken from Table 1 by ship type, size band and phase — and Table 1 prints two different phase timetables. Regulation 24.5 carries the minimum propulsion power floor.
quick_revision.major_trap: Repeating the stem's premise that Phase 2 is the present framework. At this March 2025 sitting Phase 2 has closed on both of Table 1's timetables — on 31 March 2022 for containerships and the larger gas carriers, and on 31 December 2024 for tankers, bulk carriers, reefers, combination carriers and ro-ro ships, only ten weeks before the paper. Phase 2 is still operative law for the cohort contracted into it, but it is no longer the current phase. The second trap is applying one timetable to the other's ships, which shifts a 30 per cent obligation by two years and nine months.

retrieval_cards.prompt: State the required EEDI duty and where it lives.
retrieval_cards.answer: MARPOL Annex VI regulation 24.1: for each new ship the attained EEDI shall be less than or equal to the required EEDI, which is (1 − X/100) × the reference line value. X is the reduction factor from Table 1 for the ship's type, size band and phase; the reference line comes from Table 2's parameters against DWT or GT. The attained EEDI itself is regulation 22.
retrieval_cards.why: Correct post-2021 numbering plus the formula is the frame the whole answer hangs on, and the old numbering still circulates in notes.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Give both EEDI phase timetables and say where Phase 2 stands in March 2025.
retrieval_cards.answer: Timetable one — gas carriers 15,000 DWT and above, all containerships, general cargo ships, LNG carriers, cruise passenger ships: Phase 2 ran to 31 March 2022, Phase 3 from 1 April 2022. Timetable two — bulk carriers, smaller gas bands, tankers, reefers, combination carriers, all ro-ro: Phase 2 ran to 31 December 2024, Phase 3 from 1 January 2025. So at March 2025 Phase 2 has closed on both, the second only ten weeks earlier.
retrieval_cards.why: The stem calls Phase 2 the 'present' framework. It is not, and stating the position precisely is worth marks.

retrieval_cards.prompt: If Phase 2 has closed, is it still law?
retrieval_cards.answer: Yes. A ship's required EEDI is fixed by the phase she was contracted or built into, so an expired phase continues to govern its cohort for the rest of those ships' lives — as Phase 0 and Phase 1 still do. What has changed is that Phase 2 is no longer the current phase for a ship being contracted now.
retrieval_cards.why: Holding 'closed' and 'still operative' together at once is what makes the adjudication of the printed premise correct rather than pedantic.

retrieval_cards.prompt: How should design features be organised?
retrieval_cards.answer: By which side of the equation they attack. Attained EEDI ≈ (power × SFC × carbon factor) ÷ (capacity × reference speed). So: reduce the power (hull, propeller, engine, auxiliaries); reduce the carbon factor (the fuel); recover or displace energy (waste heat, shaft generator, ESDs, air, wind); raise the denominator (capacity).
retrieval_cards.why: A list of gadgets cannot explain why any of them helps. The mechanism grouping is what earns a first-class mark.

retrieval_cards.prompt: What is the single most effective design decision for reducing attained EEDI?
retrieval_cards.answer: Two answers, both defensible and both worth stating. Structurally, reduced installed power and design speed — power appears directly in the numerator and resistance rises far faster than speed. In terms of a single component, the fuel — the carbon conversion factor is a straight multiplier, so LNG or methanol dual fuel gives the largest step from an otherwise conventional design. Qualify LNG with methane slip.
retrieval_cards.why: An examiner asking for 'the most effective' is testing whether the candidate understands the equation rather than the brochure.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Why does regulation 24.5 exist?
retrieval_cards.answer: Because the cheapest way to pass a design index built on installed power is to install less power, and a ship with too little power cannot keep steerage and manoeuvre in adverse conditions. Regulation 24.5 therefore sets a minimum propulsion power requirement, with the numerical criteria in Organization guidelines. Regulation 24.6 carries the review trigger for the phase scheme.
retrieval_cards.why: Naming the loophole and the regulation that closes it shows the candidate understands what the index measures and what it does not.

retrieval_cards.prompt: What fixes which EEDI phase a ship falls in, and where is that rule?
retrieval_cards.answer: Her construction datum, and regulation 24 does not print the rule. Regulation 2.2.18 defines 'new ship': contract on or after 1 January 2013, keel laid on or after 1 July 2013, or delivery on or after 1 July 2015. Regulation 5.4 requires a converted ship's phase to be determined for the original ship under 2.2.18, and regulation 24.2 supplies only the conversion-date datum for ship type and size. Three rules in three regulations.
retrieval_cards.why: A candidate who reads only Table 1 cannot say which phase a given ship is in, and this is a favourite oral follow-up.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Is EEDI phased in the same way as EEXI?
retrieval_cards.answer: No, and they are opposite. The phases belong to EEDI — regulation 24 Table 1, four dated phases on two timetables. EEXI is not phased: regulation 25 Table 3 sets a single fixed reduction factor per ship type and size band. The compliance routes also differ: most existing ships met EEXI by engine or shaft power limitation, which is essentially unavailable to a new build, because the required EEDI is set against the ship's own design.
retrieval_cards.why: The phase language attaches itself to EEXI in conversation, and confusing the two produces the wrong engineering for a newbuilding answer.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Why is the attained EEDI verified in two stages?
retrieval_cards.answer: Because everything in the calculation is known on paper except the speed. Preliminary verification at the design stage checks the technical file against the approved drawings; final verification at the sea trial establishes the reference speed from the measured speed-power relationship corrected to the reference condition. The Administration or an authorized organization verifies — it does not calculate and does not approve — and the IEE Certificate is issued under regulation 6 following the regulation 5.4 initial survey.
retrieval_cards.why: The stem's word is 'comply', and compliance is what verification establishes; the two-stage logic is a clean, memorable answer.

questions.short_title: Hull and Propeller Maintenance for Energy Efficiency
questions.text_verbatim: Hull & Propeller maintenance is gaining popularity with the recent high stress on the energy efficiency of ships. Write short notes on the following: (a) Hull Roughness Management. (6) (b) Condition Based Propeller Maintenance. (5) (c) Propeller Coating & Polishing. (5)
decomposition: The physical basis common to all three limbs - where the resistance actually goes and why roughness matters so much
Hull roughness management as a managed cycle: measure, predict, intervene, verify
The regulatory and guidance frame that has made it a duty rather than a preference
Condition-based propeller maintenance - what condition is monitored, how, and what triggers action
Propeller coating - what it is for, and its real limits
Propeller polishing - grades, method, and why it pays out of proportion to its cost

QP2403-Q4 (March 2024), QP2410-Q7 (October 2024) and QP2510-Q4 (October 2025) share a normalised stem with one another and ask for the merits and demerits of ducted, Kappel, contra-rotating and azimuth propellers. Nothing about blade geometry selection answers a question about roughness, condition monitoring or polishing. Topical-only; nothing taken.

QP2412-Q8 (December 2024, the SEEMP four-step energy efficiency cycle) is an EARLIER built paper and is the closest management-side relative. It supplies the framework within which hull and propeller measures are planned and evaluated, and that framing is used only as a one-line anchor in section 3. No content was taken.
