questions.verification_status: Authored fresh. This is an ENGINEERING AND OPERATIONAL question and the evidence position is stated rather than dressed up: the True Source corpus holds NO biofouling material - a whole-corpus sweep for 'biofouling' and 'hull roughness' returns nothing - and holds no IACS or class document (RQ-36). The physical content is therefore ESTABLISHED NAVAL ARCHITECTURE AND MARINE ENGINEERING and is stated as such: the decomposition of resistance, the mechanism by which roughness thickens the boundary layer and raises frictional resistance, the behaviour of antifouling coating systems, the propulsive efficiency chain and the effect of blade surface condition on torque and thrust are engineering fact and depend on no instrument. The IMO Biofouling Guidelines are cited BY IDENTITY AND EFFECT ONLY - they are GUIDANCE, not law, they are not held by the corpus and were not read, and NO resolution number, edition or paragraph is asserted. The AFS Convention is named only for the boundary it draws on coating chemistry, and its cybutryne control - whose 1 January 2023 entry into force predates this sitting by more than two years - is stated as operative without asserting any AFS provision number, since the corpus does not hold that Convention either. The one regulatory anchor that IS corpus-backed is the SEEMP duty under the revised MARPOL Annex VI, which the corpus's frozen canonical records carry and which QP2502-Q6 established for the immediately preceding sitting; it is used as the framework that makes hull and propeller management a documented obligation rather than a preference. NO quantified power penalty, fuel saving, roughness-to-power conversion or interval is asserted as a number anywhere in this object: those figures are hull-specific, coating-specific and trade-specific, and most published values originate in maker's or service-provider material.
sources: ENGINEERING FACT - the decomposition of a ship's resistance into frictional resistance, which dominates at normal merchant-ship speeds and is the component roughness acts on, and residuary resistance comprising wave-making and form effects. Roughness increases the momentum deficit in the turbulent boundary layer, thickening it and raising skin friction; the effect is a function of both the height and the texture and spacing of the roughness, which is why biological fouling is far more damaging than an equivalent height of physical roughness.

ENGINEERING FACT - the two kinds of hull roughness: physical roughness, which is permanent or semi-permanent - plate waviness, weld seams, corrosion pitting, mechanical damage, coating breakdown, over-applied or badly applied coating, and the accumulated roughness of successive coating layers; and biological roughness, which is fouling and is recoverable - slime, weed, and hard shell fouling such as barnacles and tubeworm.

ENGINEERING FACT - average hull roughness as the conventional measure, taken as a mean apparent amplitude over a defined sampling length with a hull roughness gauge at a defined pattern of stations, used to track the hull's condition dry-docking to dry-docking.

ENGINEERING FACT - antifouling coating system types and their working principle: self-polishing copolymers, which hydrolyse at a controlled rate to expose fresh biocide and to maintain a smooth surface; controlled-depletion systems; and biocide-free foul-release silicone or fluoropolymer systems, which work by presenting a low-surface-energy, low-adhesion surface from which fouling is removed by the ship's own motion above a threshold speed, and which are therefore activity-dependent.

ENGINEERING FACT - the propulsive efficiency chain: open-water efficiency, hull efficiency and relative rotative efficiency, and the effect of blade surface condition on the section's lift and drag, hence on torque absorbed, thrust delivered and the propeller's operating point relative to the engine. A roughened or fouled blade absorbs more torque for the same revolutions, so the engine is loaded earlier - a heavy running condition observable from the engine itself.

ENGINEERING FACT - blade surface condition and its causes: biological fouling, calcareous deposits, cavitation erosion characteristically on the suction face near the leading edge and tip, impingement and corrosion pitting, edge damage from debris or ice, and the roughness left by grinding or by a previous poor polish.

ENGINEERING FACT - the surface-finish grade convention used in propeller work, in which a defined roughness grade is specified for the blade surface and the leading-edge region is treated to a finer standard than the mid-chord, because the leading edge governs the section's inflow behaviour.

AUTHORITATIVE SECONDARY - the SEEMP duty under the revised MARPOL Annex VI, resolution MEPC.328(76), in force 1 November 2022: every ship keeps on board a ship-specific ship energy efficiency management plan, and hull and propeller measures are planned, implemented, monitored and evaluated within it. The regulation is corpus-held and was established for the immediately preceding sitting; the associated Organization guidelines were not read and no guideline edition is asserted.

AUTHORITATIVE SECONDARY - the operational carbon intensity regime, under which in-service hull and propeller condition affects the attained annual operational carbon intensity and therefore the ship's rating. Named as the commercial driver that has made this maintenance a board-level matter; no rating boundary or reduction factor is quoted.

AUTHORITATIVE SECONDARY - the IMO Biofouling Guidelines, cited by identity and effect only: guidance, not law, recommending a ship-specific biofouling management plan and record book, and covering the selection and maintenance of the antifouling system, the treatment of niche areas and the management of in-water inspection and cleaning. Not held by the corpus; no resolution number, edition or paragraph is asserted.

AUTHORITATIVE SECONDARY - the AFS Convention, named for the boundary it draws on coating chemistry: the prohibition of organotin compounds acting as biocides in antifouling systems, and the later control on cybutryne, which took effect on 1 January 2023 - more than two years before this sitting - and is therefore operative here. The Convention is not held by the corpus and no article or annex provision is asserted.

INDUSTRY PRACTICE - in-water inspection and cleaning practice: diver and remotely operated inspection, brush-cart and rotating-brush cleaning, soft-brush and water-jet systems for foul-release coatings, proactive grooming of light slime as an alternative to reactive cleaning of established fouling, capture and filtration of cleaning debris, and the fact that port States increasingly regulate in-water cleaning for invasive-species and biocide-release reasons and that permission is not automatic.

ENGINEERING JUDGEMENT - the performance-monitoring method: normalising measured shaft power, revolutions, speed through water and fuel consumption for draught, trim, sea state, wind, current and water temperature, and tracking the residual trend rather than raw figures.
unresolved: NO QUANTIFIED PENALTY OR SAVING IS ASSERTED ANYWHERE IN THIS OBJECT. No power increase per unit of roughness, no fuel penalty for a given fouling condition, no percentage saving from polishing and no payback period is stated. These figures are hull-specific, coating-specific, speed-specific and trade-specific, and the published values originate very largely in coating-maker and cleaning-contractor material that is not independently verified. The mechanisms are given instead, and every mark in this answer is available without a number.

NO RESOLUTION NUMBER, EDITION OR PARAGRAPH OF THE IMO BIOFOULING GUIDELINES IS ASSERTED. The corpus holds no biofouling material of any kind - a whole-corpus sweep returns nothing - and the Guidelines were not read. They are cited by identity and effect and their non-mandatory status is stated expressly.

NO AFS CONVENTION PROVISION IS ASSERTED. The Convention is not held by the corpus. The organotin prohibition and the cybutryne control are stated as the boundary they draw on coating chemistry, with the cybutryne effective date of 1 January 2023, and no article or annex reference is given.

NO NUMERIC AVERAGE HULL ROUGHNESS VALUE, ACCEPTANCE THRESHOLD OR SURFACE-FINISH GRADE VALUE IS QUOTED. The measurement convention and the grading principle are described; the numbers are specification- and society-specific and no class rulebook or standard is held (RQ-36).

NO INTERVAL IS PRESCRIBED FOR PROPELLER POLISHING OR IN-WATER INSPECTION. The whole point of condition-based maintenance is that the interval is set by measured condition rather than by the calendar, and asserting a fixed interval would contradict limb (b).
WHETHER IN-WATER CLEANING IS PERMITTED IN A GIVEN PORT IS A LOCAL REGULATORY QUESTION. The answer states that permission is required and is not automatic, and asserts no national or port requirement.

blocks.h: 1. The physical basis common to all three limbs

blocks.p: All three short notes are about one thing: keeping the ship's underwater surfaces hydrodynamically smooth. Establishing why that matters, in three sentences, makes every later point scorable.

ul: A merchant ship's resistance divides into frictional resistance and residuary resistance. At normal merchant-ship speeds friction dominates, and friction is the component that surface condition acts on.

Roughness works by increasing the momentum deficit in the turbulent boundary layer, thickening it and raising skin friction. The penalty depends not only on the height of the roughness but on its texture and spacing, which is why biological fouling is far more damaging than physical roughness of the same height — slime and weed disturb the flow out of all proportion to their thickness.

The consequence is measured in the engine room: for the same speed the ship needs more shaft power, so more fuel and more CO2; or at constant power she loses speed. On the propeller the same roughness raises absorbed torque, so the engine runs heavy and reaches its limit earlier.

blocks.h: (a) Hull Roughness Management — 6 marks
2. What is being managed, and the cycle that manages it

blocks.p: Two kinds of roughness, and they behave completely differently.

rows: Plate waviness, weld seams, corrosion pitting, mechanical damage, coating breakdown, badly applied or over-thick coating, accumulated coating layers
Slime, weed, and hard fouling - barnacles, tubeworm, mussels
Permanent or semi-permanent; tends to ratchet upward over the ship's life
Recoverable - it can be removed and the surface restored
Surface preparation, coating specification and application quality at dry-dock
Antifouling system selection, activity profile, inspection and cleaning

blocks.p: Hull roughness management is the deliberate cycle by which both are held down. Four steps, and writing them as a cycle rather than a list is what earns the six marks.

ol: Measure. Average hull roughness is taken at dry-dock with a hull roughness gauge at a defined pattern of stations, as a mean apparent amplitude over a defined sampling length, and tracked dock to dock so the trend is visible. In service the equivalent measurement is performance monitoring — shaft power, revolutions, speed through water and fuel consumption, normalised for draught, trim, wind, sea state, current and water temperature, with the residual trend watched rather than the raw figures. Unnormalised data is the commonest reason a hull-performance programme tells the owner nothing.

Specify and apply the coating properly. Surface preparation to the specified standard, correct film thickness, correct conditions and correct overcoating intervals. Application quality is a roughness decision: an over-applied or badly applied coating leaves the ship rougher than it found her, and successive layers over a ship's life ratchet roughness upward, which is why full blasting back to steel is periodically the right answer however expensive it looks.

Choose the system for the ship's actual trade. Self-polishing copolymer systems hydrolyse at a controlled rate to expose fresh biocide and maintain smoothness. Foul-release silicone or fluoropolymer systems carry no biocide and work by presenting a low-adhesion surface from which fouling is shed by the ship's own motion — excellent for a fast, continuously trading ship and poor for one that idles, because they are activity-dependent. Trading pattern, speed, idle time and water temperature decide the choice, not the brochure.

Inspect, intervene and verify. Diver or remotely operated inspection of the hull and, critically, of niche areas — sea chests and gratings, bow and stern thruster tunnels, rudder and stabiliser recesses, bilge keels, propeller boss and the rope guard — which foul first and are routinely omitted. Then in-water cleaning where justified, and proactive grooming of light slime, which is gentler on the coating and cheaper than reactive cleaning of established hard fouling. Verify the intervention against the performance trend, because a clean that produces no measurable recovery has told you the problem was elsewhere.

blocks.p: Two practical constraints must be stated. Aggressive mechanical cleaning damages the coating and can leave the hull rougher and foul faster afterwards, so method must be matched to coating type — soft brushes or water jets for foul-release systems. And in-water cleaning is increasingly regulated by port and coastal States, for invasive-species and biocide-release reasons: permission is required and is not automatic, and capture and filtration of the debris is often a condition.

blocks.h: 3. Why it has become a duty rather than a preference

blocks.p: The stem's own words — 'the recent high stress on the energy efficiency of ships' — invite this, and it is a mark.

ul: The SEEMP. Under the revised MARPOL Annex VI, resolution MEPC.328(76) (in force 1 November 2022), every ship keeps a ship-specific ship energy efficiency management plan. Hull and propeller measures are planned, implemented, monitored and evaluated within it, so the work is documented and auditable rather than discretionary.

Operational carbon intensity. In-service hull and propeller condition directly affects the ship's attained annual operational carbon intensity and therefore her rating, which is commercial and visible to charterers. This is what turned hull husbandry from an engineering preference into a board-level matter.

The Biofouling Guidelines. The IMO's guidance on biofouling recommends a ship-specific biofouling management plan and record book, covering the antifouling system, niche areas and in-water inspection and cleaning. It is guidance and not law, and saying so is part of the answer — but it is what port States and charterers increasingly expect to see.

The AFS Convention sets the boundary on chemistry: organotin compounds are prohibited as biocides in antifouling systems, and the control on cybutryne took effect on 1 January 2023 and is operative. A coating choice is therefore constrained by law as well as by trade.

blocks.h: (b) Condition Based Propeller Maintenance — 5 marks
4. Monitoring the condition, and letting it set the interval

blocks.p: Condition-based maintenance means the propeller is worked on when its measured condition says so, not when the calendar says so. That single sentence is the definition, and everything else is how the condition is measured.
What is monitored, in three groups:

ol: Performance indicators from the ship herself. The propeller declares its own condition through the machinery. Watch the power–speed–revolution relationship: a fouled or roughened blade absorbs more torque at the same revolutions, so the engine runs heavy — higher torque and load for given revolutions, exhaust temperatures up, turbocharger speed up, and the load limit reached earlier. Track slip, and shaft power against revolutions from a torsion meter where fitted. All of it must be normalised for draught, trim, weather and current before it means anything.

Direct inspection. Diver or ROV inspection of the blades, boss and rope guard, photographed and graded, and inspection at dry-dock. What is being looked for is fouling and calcareous deposit, cavitation erosion — characteristically on the suction face near the leading edge and the tip — impingement and corrosion pitting, edge damage from debris or ice, and the roughness left by an earlier poor polish or grind.

Machinery condition indicators. Shaft and stern tube bearing wear-down, stern tube oil condition and consumption, seal performance, and shaft vibration signature — because a damaged or unevenly fouled blade is unbalanced and says so through blade-rate vibration. Increasing bearing temperature or an oil sample loaded with bearing metal is propeller-shaft news as much as bearing news.

blocks.p: What the monitoring produces: a trigger rather than a date. When the normalised performance trend degrades past the agreed threshold, or an inspection grades the blade surface below the agreed standard, the intervention — polish, repair, or dock — is scheduled. The economic argument is straightforward: intervention is cheap, the fuel penalty of leaving it is continuous, and the whole point is to spend the money at the moment it repays fastest.

Say what condition-based maintenance is being compared against, because the contrast is the mark: it replaces calendar-based polishing at every dock or every fixed number of months, which either wastes money on a clean propeller or leaves a fouled one running for months.

And state the limits honestly. Condition monitoring needs reliable, normalised data and a baseline — without both, the trend is noise; it needs an agreed threshold, or the trigger is a matter of opinion; and access for inspection or in-water polishing depends on port permission, water clarity, current and diver safety, so a trigger cannot always be acted on when it fires.

blocks.h: (c) Propeller Coating & Polishing — 5 marks
5. Propeller coating - purpose and real limits

blocks.p: Purpose. A propeller coating is applied to the blades and boss to resist fouling and corrosion and to hold a smooth surface for longer, so that the interval between polishes lengthens and the average surface condition across the docking cycle is better.

ul: The systems used are typically biocide-free foul-release types — silicone or fluoropolymer — chosen because they present a low-surface-energy, low-adhesion surface from which fouling releases under the very high water velocities at the blade. Hard, smooth non-stick coatings are also used.

Application demands more than the hull: the blades must be fully cleaned and prepared, usually blasted and profiled, and coated in controlled conditions at correct film thickness. An improperly applied coating is worse than none, because it will detach unevenly and leave a surface rougher than the bare bronze.
Benefits: slower fouling, lower average roughness across the cycle, longer polish intervals, easier cleaning when it is done, and some protection against corrosion and calcareous deposition.

blocks.p: The limits, which must be stated for the answer to be credible. The blade is the most hydrodynamically hostile surface on the ship: high tip velocities, cyclic loading, cavitation and impingement. Coatings therefore wear preferentially at the leading edge and the tip, exactly where surface condition matters most, and cavitation erosion will remove them locally regardless of quality. A coating is a life-extender between polishes, not a substitute for polishing, it requires periodic reapplication in dock, and its cost must be justified against the ship's actual trade.

blocks.h: 6. Propeller polishing - method, grades and why it pays

blocks.p: What it is. The controlled removal of fouling, calcareous deposit and surface roughness from the blades, restoring a specified surface finish. It is done in water by divers with rotating discs and progressively finer abrasive pads, or in dry-dock to a higher and more consistent standard.
Method, in the order it is done:

ol: Remove fouling and calcareous deposit from the whole blade, both faces, plus the boss and the rope guard — areas routinely skipped in a hurried in-water job.

Work through progressively finer grades to the specified finish, never leaving the surface with the coarse directional scratching of a single-grade grind, which can be worse than the fouling it replaced.

Give particular attention to the leading edge and the outer radii. The leading edge governs the section's inflow behaviour and the outer radii do most of the work, so the finish there is specified finer than at mid-chord and matters most.

Do not reshape the blade. Polishing removes surface material only. Dressing edge damage, correcting pitch or repairing cavitation erosion is propeller repair, requires an approved procedure and class involvement where classed items are affected, and is a different job with different consequences.
Record it — grade achieved, photographs, areas treated — and verify against the performance trend, which closes the condition-based loop from limb (b).

blocks.p: Why it pays out of proportion to its cost. Three reasons, and giving them turns a description into an argument.

ul: The propeller is a small area doing a large job. The blades are a tiny fraction of the wetted surface but they operate at very high relative velocity and they set the efficiency of the entire propulsion chain, so roughness there costs more per square metre than anywhere else on the ship.
A polish is cheap, quick and can be done in water without taking the ship out of service, while the fuel penalty it removes is continuous, every hour, until it is done.

It unloads the engine. Restoring the blade surface lightens the running condition, moves the operating point back toward the design point and recovers margin the ship had lost — which matters for both fuel and for the ship's operational carbon intensity.

blocks.p: The closing judgement, which ties the three limbs together: hull and propeller maintenance is the cheapest energy-efficiency measure available to a ship in service. It requires no capital modification, no approval and no dry-docking, and unlike a design change it can be done again next month. What it requires instead is measurement — and that is why all three limbs of this question are really about knowing the condition of a surface you cannot see.

blocks.h: Why this structure scores

blocks.p: 'Write short notes' invites three disconnected paragraphs, which is how most candidates lose marks here. Section 1 defeats that by establishing the physics once — friction dominates, roughness thickens the boundary layer, texture matters more than height — so that all three limbs can refer back to a single mechanism instead of each asserting that roughness is bad.

The second structural decision is that limb (a) is written as a cycle: measure, specify, choose, intervene and verify. Six marks for a topic called 'management' should be a management answer, and a cycle is a management answer where a list is not.

blocks.h: The one physical fact worth more than any number

blocks.p: The penalty from roughness depends on its texture and spacing as much as its height, which is why slime and weed cost far more than physical roughness of the same thickness. That single sentence explains why a hull that measures acceptably at dock can still be losing badly in service, why light fouling is worth removing early, and why proactive grooming beats reactive cleaning. It is also the reason the answer needs no percentage figures to make its case.

blocks.h: Physical versus biological roughness

rows: Plate waviness, weld seams, corrosion pitting, mechanical damage, coating breakdown, over-thick or poor application, accumulated layers
Largely NO - it ratchets upward over the ship's life
Dry-dock: surface preparation, specification, application quality
In service: coating choice, activity, inspection, cleaning
Cleaning or grooming, and the right antifouling system

blocks.p: Candidates who know only the fouling half cannot explain why an owner would ever blast a hull back to bare steel.

blocks.h: Matching the coating to the trade

ul: Self-polishing copolymer — hydrolyses at a controlled rate, exposing fresh biocide and maintaining smoothness. Tolerant of idle time.
Controlled depletion — the older, simpler biocidal route.

Foul-release silicone or fluoropolymer — no biocide, works by low adhesion, and needs the ship's own motion to shed fouling. Excellent for a fast, continuously trading ship; poor for one that idles, and easily damaged by aggressive cleaning.

blocks.p: The examinable point is that this is a trade decision, not a product decision: speed, idle time, water temperature and trading pattern choose the system.

blocks.h: Common mistakes

ul: Writing three unconnected notes with no common physical basis.
Treating hull roughness as fouling only, and missing physical roughness and its ratchet effect.
Quoting a percentage fuel penalty or saving from memory. Those figures are hull-, coating- and trade-specific and mostly come from maker's material.
Recommending aggressive mechanical cleaning without saying that it damages the coating and can leave the hull fouling faster.
Ignoring niche areas — sea chests, thruster tunnels, rudder and bilge-keel recesses, rope guard — which foul first.
Describing performance monitoring with no normalisation for draught, trim, weather and current. Unnormalised data is noise.
Answering limb (b) as 'inspect the propeller regularly', which is calendar-based maintenance and the opposite of what was asked.
Confusing polishing with repair. Polishing removes surface material; reshaping, edge dressing and pitch correction are repair and need approval.
Presenting a propeller coating as a substitute for polishing. It lengthens the interval; it does not replace it.
Assuming in-water cleaning is always permitted. Port and coastal States increasingly regulate it.

blocks.h: Examiner traps

ul: 'Condition Based' in limb (b) is the whole limb. The examiner is testing whether the candidate knows that the interval is set by measured condition, not by the calendar. An answer describing routine inspection has answered a different question.

'Coating & Polishing' is limb (c) and it is two topics for five marks. Both must appear, and the relationship between them — coating lengthens the polish interval, it does not replace polishing — is what ties them together.

The stem's 'recent high stress on the energy efficiency of ships' is an invitation to name the regulatory drivers. The SEEMP and the operational carbon intensity regime are worth marks; so is knowing that the Biofouling Guidelines are guidance, not law.
Limb (a) is worth 6 and the others 5. Write the extra content in (a), where the marks are, not in whichever limb you know best.
This is an Engineering Management paper, so the measurement, verification and decision-making content is the point, not a catalogue of cleaning equipment.

blocks.h: Likely oral follow-up

ul: Why does slime cost more than an equivalent thickness of physical roughness?
Your engine is running heavy at the same draught and weather. What do you suspect and how do you confirm it?
What is average hull roughness and how is it measured?
You have a foul-release coating and the ship has been idle for six weeks. What has happened?
How would you decide when to polish the propeller?
Where does cavitation erosion appear on a blade, and why there?
What is the difference between polishing and repairing a propeller?
Can you clean the hull in this port? What would you need?
Which instrument requires your ship to have a plan for this, and is the Biofouling Guidance mandatory?

blocks.h: Memory framework

blocks.p: One physical fact and three cycles. Friction dominates; texture beats height (1).
Limb (a): MEASURE, SPECIFY, CHOOSE, INTERVENE, VERIFY (2). Limb (b): SHIP SAYS, DIVER SEES, MACHINERY TELLS → TRIGGER, NOT DATE (4). Limb (c): COAT TO LENGTHEN, POLISH TO RESTORE (5, 6).

blocks.h: Uncertainty and evidence limits

blocks.p: The corpus holds no biofouling material at all — a whole-corpus sweep for 'biofouling' and 'hull roughness' returns nothing — and it holds no IACS or class document (RQ-36). The IMO Biofouling Guidelines are therefore cited by identity and effect only, with their non-mandatory status stated expressly, and no resolution number, edition or paragraph is asserted. The AFS Convention is likewise not held and no article or annex provision is asserted; the cybutryne control is stated with its 1 January 2023 effective date, which predates this sitting by more than two years.

No quantified penalty or saving appears anywhere in this answer — no power increase per unit of roughness, no fuel penalty for a fouling condition, no percentage recovery from polishing, no payback period, no roughness threshold and no surface-finish grade value. Those figures are hull-, coating-, speed- and trade-specific, and the published values originate very largely in coating-maker and cleaning-contractor material. The mechanisms are given instead, and every mark is available without a number.

No maintenance interval is prescribed, which is not an omission but a consequence of limb (b): the whole point of condition-based maintenance is that the interval is set by measured condition, and asserting a fixed one would contradict the answer.

benefits: slower fouling, lower average roughness across the cycle, easier cleaning, some corrosion protection
LIMITS: coatings wear preferentially at leading edge and tip, exactly where it matters most, and cavitation removes them locally
a coating is a life-extender between polishes, not a substitute for polishing

steps.title: Propeller polishing - method, grades and why it pays
points: controlled removal of fouling, calcareous deposit and roughness to a specified finish, in water by divers or in dock to a higher standard
remove deposit from both faces plus boss and rope guard - the areas skipped in a hurried job
work through progressively finer grades; never leave coarse directional scratching
particular attention to the leading edge and outer radii, which are specified finer because they do the work
DO NOT RESHAPE - dressing edge damage, pitch correction and cavitation repair are propeller REPAIR, needing approved procedures and class involvement
record the grade and verify against the performance trend, closing the loop from limb (b)
why it pays: a small area at high relative velocity setting the whole chain's efficiency; cheap, quick and done in water; and it unloads the engine
closing judgement: the cheapest energy-efficiency measure available in service, and it is really about measurement

questions.memory_cue: One physical fact and three cycles. Friction dominates, texture beats height (1). Then MEASURE, SPECIFY, CHOOSE, INTERVENE, VERIFY (2); SHIP SAYS, DIVER SEES, MACHINERY TELLS — trigger, not date (4); and COAT TO LENGTHEN, POLISH TO RESTORE (5, 6).

quick_revision.recall_15s: Friction dominates at merchant-ship speeds, and roughness thickens the boundary layer — texture and spacing matter as much as height, so slime costs more than physical roughness of the same thickness. (a) Two roughnesses: physical (irrecoverable, ratchets up) and biological (recoverable). Cycle: measure → specify → choose → intervene → verify, with normalised performance data and niche areas inspected. Drivers: SEEMP (MEPC.328(76)), carbon intensity, Biofouling Guidelines — guidance not law, AFS cybutryne from 1 Jan 2023. (b) Condition sets the interval, not the calendar — heavy running, diver inspection, vibration and bearing data → a trigger. (c) Coating lengthens the interval; polishing restores the surface — progressive grades, leading edge finest, and polishing is not repair.
critical_numbers: AFS cybutryne control took effect 1 JANUARY 2023 - more than two years before this sitting, therefore operative
Revised MARPOL Annex VI, MEPC.328(76), in force 1 NOVEMBER 2022 - the SEEMP duty
Mark split 6 + 5 + 5: hull roughness management carries the extra mark
NO fuel penalty, saving, roughness threshold, finish grade or maintenance interval is quoted - all are hull-, coating- and trade-specific
quick_revision.critical_regulation: The SEEMP under the revised MARPOL Annex VI, resolution MEPC.328(76), in force 1 November 2022: every ship keeps a ship-specific energy efficiency management plan, and hull and propeller measures are planned, implemented, monitored and evaluated within it — which is what makes this work documented and auditable. The IMO Biofouling Guidelines are guidance, not law. The AFS Convention constrains the chemistry: organotin prohibited, cybutryne controlled from 1 January 2023.
quick_revision.major_trap: Answering limb (b) as 'inspect the propeller regularly'. That is calendar-based maintenance and the exact opposite of what was asked: condition-based maintenance means the measured condition sets the interval, through normalised performance data, inspection grading and machinery indicators, producing a trigger rather than a date. The second trap is quoting a percentage fuel penalty or saving — those figures are hull-, coating- and trade-specific and mostly originate in maker's material.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Why does slime cost more than physical roughness of the same height?
retrieval_cards.answer: Because the penalty depends on the roughness's texture and spacing as well as its height. Biological fouling disturbs the turbulent boundary layer out of all proportion to its thickness, thickening it and raising skin friction far more than smooth physical roughness of the same amplitude. That is why light fouling is worth removing early and why proactive grooming beats reactive cleaning.
retrieval_cards.why: The single physical fact that makes the whole answer coherent, and it requires no numbers.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Distinguish physical from biological hull roughness.
retrieval_cards.answer: Physical — plate waviness, weld seams, corrosion pitting, mechanical damage, coating breakdown, over-thick or poor application, and the accumulation of successive coating layers. Largely irrecoverable; it ratchets upward over the ship's life, and the ultimate remedy is full blasting back to steel. Biological — slime, weed and hard fouling. Recoverable by cleaning, and controlled by coating choice, activity and inspection.
retrieval_cards.why: Candidates who know only the fouling half cannot explain why an owner would ever blast a hull back to bare steel.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Give the hull roughness management cycle.
retrieval_cards.answer: Measure — average hull roughness at dock, and in-service performance monitoring normalised for draught, trim, weather and current. Specify — surface preparation, film thickness and application quality. Choose — the antifouling system matched to speed, idle time and trade. Intervene — inspection including niche areas, grooming rather than reactive cleaning. Verify — against the performance trend.
retrieval_cards.why: Six marks for a topic called 'management' demands a management answer, and a cycle is one where a list is not.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Your ship has a foul-release coating and has been idle six weeks. What has happened?
retrieval_cards.answer: She has probably fouled. Foul-release silicone and fluoropolymer coatings carry no biocide — they work by presenting a low-surface-energy, low-adhesion surface from which fouling is shed by the ship's own motion above a threshold speed. They are activity-dependent, so they perform excellently on a fast continuous trader and poorly on a ship that idles. Cleaning must then use soft brushes or water jets, because aggressive mechanical cleaning damages the coating.
retrieval_cards.why: The examinable point is that coating selection is a trade decision, not a product decision.

retrieval_cards.prompt: What does 'condition based' mean for propeller maintenance, and what is it replacing?
retrieval_cards.answer: The propeller is worked on when its measured condition says so, not when the calendar says so. The monitoring produces a trigger — a normalised performance trend or an inspection grade crossing an agreed threshold — rather than a date. It replaces calendar-based polishing at every dock or every fixed number of months, which either wastes money on a clean propeller or leaves a fouled one running for months.
retrieval_cards.why: The whole of limb (b) turns on this, and describing routine inspection answers a different question.

retrieval_cards.prompt: How does the ship tell you the propeller needs attention?
retrieval_cards.answer: Through heavy running. A fouled or roughened blade absorbs more torque at the same revolutions, so for a given speed torque and load rise, exhaust temperatures and turbocharger speed rise, and the load limit is reached earlier. Watch the power–speed–revolution relationship, slip, and shaft power from a torsion meter — all normalised for draught, trim, weather and current, or the data is noise. Confirm by diver or ROV inspection.
retrieval_cards.why: The single most practical and most examinable diagnostic in the question, and a standard oral follow-up.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Where does cavitation erosion appear on a blade, and what does it mean for coating?
retrieval_cards.answer: Characteristically on the suction face near the leading edge and the tip. It matters for limb (c) because that is exactly where a propeller coating wears preferentially and where cavitation will remove it locally regardless of quality — which is why a coating is a life-extender between polishes, not a substitute for polishing.
retrieval_cards.why: It links limbs (b) and (c) with one physical observation and prevents the common overclaim about coatings.

retrieval_cards.prompt: What is the boundary between propeller polishing and propeller repair?
retrieval_cards.answer: Polishing removes surface material only — fouling, calcareous deposit and roughness — working through progressively finer grades to a specified finish, with the leading edge and outer radii finished finest. Repair is anything that changes the blade: dressing edge damage, correcting pitch, or making good cavitation erosion. Repair needs an approved procedure and class involvement where classed items are affected.
retrieval_cards.why: Confusing the two is both an exam error and a real engineering one, and the boundary is worth a mark on its own.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Can you just clean the hull in the next port?
retrieval_cards.answer: Not automatically. In-water cleaning is increasingly regulated by port and coastal States for invasive species and biocide release reasons; permission is required and capture and filtration of the debris is often a condition. The method must also suit the coating — aggressive mechanical cleaning damages it and can leave the hull fouling faster than before.
retrieval_cards.why: A practical constraint that turns a textbook recommendation into an operational answer.

questions.short_title: Collision off the Indian Coast - Action under the Merchant Shipping Act
questions.text_verbatim: An Indian flag vessel collided with another vessel off the coast of India, resulting in the loss of lives, vessel damage, and an oil spill. In accordance with the provisions under the Merchant Shipping Act, what steps should be initiated and who should initiate such steps for the safety of the ships and the marine environment. (16)
decomposition: What has actually happened, in legal terms - four distinct events in one casualty, each with its own machinery
The immediate duties on the Master and on the ship, and who owes them
The reporting chain - to whom, by whom, and under what obligation
Steps for the safety of the ships - salvage, refuge, and the State's power to intervene
Steps for the marine environment - the national response machinery and the Central Government's directions power
Investigation and inquiry - the two systems, national and international, and which is engaged here
Liability, compensation and the certificates that fund the response

The closing sentence is reproduced VERBATIM between the two papers: 'In accordance with the provisions under the Merchant Shipping Act, what steps should be initiated and who should initiate such steps for the safety of the ships and the marine environment.' DIRECTION OF TRAVEL IS BACKWARD IN TIME AND THEREFORE SAFE - February 2024 precedes March 2025 by thirteen months.

THE SCENARIO IS MATERIALLY DIFFERENT AND THE DIFFERENCE IS MOST OF THE ANSWER. The donor is a GROUNDING with the owners having ABANDONED the property - which engages wreck and salvage and the abandonment machinery. This paper is a COLLISION WITH LOSS OF LIFE, vessel damage and an oil spill, with no abandonment. Three consequences: a second ship is involved throughout, so collision duties and the other vessel's flag State enter; LOSS OF LIFE makes the casualty a VERY SERIOUS MARINE CASUALTY, which changes the investigation obligation from recommended practice to a mandatory marine safety investigation; and the wreck and abandonment material that carries much of the donor is largely inapplicable here.

WHAT WAS TAKEN: the statutory machinery that is common to both - the Part XA pollution provisions and the Central Government's power to give directions, the wreck and salvage Part where it applies, the unseaworthy-and-unsafe-ships detention power, the places of refuge guidance resolution A.1184(33), and the Casualty Investigation Code as the international layer. WHAT WAS NOT TAKEN: the abandonment analysis, the wreck-removal-centred structure, and every sitting-relative statement, all of which were re-authored.

THE DONOR'S OWN TEMPORAL RECORD WAS READ AND ITS CENTRAL WARNING IS ADOPTED. It records that QP2607-Q7 - a fully solved question on the Merchant Shipping Act 2025, the same statute title and the superficially obvious donor for any Indian merchant shipping question - WAS EXAMINED AND REJECTED OUTRIGHT. The same rejection applies here and for the same reason: the 2025 Act commenced 15 March 2026, twelve and a half months after this sitting.

QP2512-Q5 (December 2025, Indian inquiries into casualties on FOREIGN ships) was the second-strongest match at 0.31 and was REJECTED ON DIRECTION OF TRAVEL - it is a later sitting - and on scope, since this casualty involves an Indian flag vessel and the investigation question is therefore a flag State question first.

QP2508-Q5, QP2506-Q9 and QP2410-Q1 (unseaworthy and unsafe ships under the MS Act 1958) share the detention machinery. QP2410-Q1 is earlier and was used only to confirm that the detention power sits where the donor places it; nothing was taken.

blocks.h: 1. What has actually happened - four events in one casualty

blocks.p: Begin by separating the incident into its legal components, because each triggers different machinery and different people, and the stem asks who as well as what.

ol: A collision — engaging the duties of both masters and the law of collision.
Loss of life — which, as section 6 shows, converts the casualty into a very serious marine casualty and makes a safety investigation mandatory.
Damage to the vessels — engaging seaworthiness, survey, class, detention and possibly salvage.
An oil spill — engaging the pollution response machinery, the Central Government's directions power and the liability conventions.

blocks.p: The statute is the Merchant Shipping Act, 1958. It governs at this sitting and throughout the response to this casualty.

And note the constant that runs through the whole answer: the Act is enabling as much as it is prohibitory. Most of what follows is the Central Government and the Director-General of Shipping being given power to direct, and the owner, master and salvor being obliged to comply.

blocks.h: 2. Immediate steps on board - the Master, and the order matters

blocks.p: The first steps are the Master's, and they are taken before any authority is involved. The order is life, then ship, then environment, then evidence.

ol: Muster, account for all persons, and search for the missing. With loss of life reported, this is the first and overriding duty.

Render assistance to the other vessel and to persons in danger, so far as he can do so without serious danger to his own ship and those on board, and stand by. Exchange the identifying particulars of ship, port of registry and ports of departure and destination. This duty is in the Act and is not discretionary.
Sound tanks and compartments, assess damage, contain flooding, and assess the ship's stability and residual strength before any decision to move.

Stop the source of the spill — isolate the damaged tank, transfer internally where it is safe to do so, close valves and pump out to intact spaces. Deploy the ship's SOPEP equipment and act on the plan.
Broadcast and report — distress or urgency as appropriate, and a danger message where the casualty is a hazard to navigation.

Preserve evidence. Secure the voyage data recorder, charts, logs, engine records, alarm and printout records, and record the position, time and circumstances. This is the step candidates omit and it decides both the investigation and the liability that follows.

blocks.h: 3. The reporting chain - who tells whom

blocks.p: The reports go outward in parallel, not in sequence, and each has a different addressee and purpose.

rows: The company's emergency response is activated under the ISM safety management system
Directorate General of Shipping, through the nearest Mercantile Marine Department
The casualty report to the flag State administration under the Act - the statutory trigger for inquiry
Indian Coast Guard and the nearest coastal radio station / MRCC
Search and rescue for the lives lost, and the pollution response at sea
Nearest coastal State authority and port authority
The spill is in India's maritime zones and coastal interests are engaged
To appoint surveyors and correspondents, and to fund the response - see Q5 and Q6 on this paper
Damage survey and conditions of class before the ship moves or trades
Other vessel's flag State, if foreign
Substantially interested State, for the investigation - see section 6

blocks.p: Alongside the national obligations sit the international ones: a MARPOL Protocol I report on an incident involving harmful substances, and a SOLAS chapter V danger message where the casualty endangers navigation.

blocks.h: 4. Steps for the safety of the ships

blocks.p: The stem asks expressly about the safety of the ships, and the machinery here is largely about the State's power to compel.

ol: Damage assessment and survey. The classification society and the Administration survey the damage. Repairs, temporary or permanent, are approved before the ship proceeds, and conditions of class or a short-term certificate may be imposed.

Detention. The Act's unseaworthy and unsafe ships provisions — sections 334 to 336 — empower the Administration to detain a ship that is unsafe by reason of defective condition of hull or machinery, undermanning, overloading or improper loading. A damaged ship after a collision is squarely within that power, and the initiator is the Director-General of Shipping or the surveyor acting for him.

Salvage. If the ship cannot proceed under her own power, salvage services are engaged — commercially by the owner, ordinarily on Lloyd's Open Form terms with its no-cure-no-pay basis and its environmental provisions. The Act's wreck and salvage Part, sections 390 to 404, and the Merchant Shipping (Wrecks and Salvage) Rules, 1974, provide the statutory framework and the receiver of wreck's functions where wreck arises.

A place of refuge. If she must be moved to sheltered water, the request is made to the coastal State. The current guidance is resolution A.1184(33), Guidelines on places of refuge for ships in need of assistance, adopted by the 33rd Assembly on 6 December 2023 and revoking A.949(23). The decision is the coastal State's, taken on an objective analysis of the risks of granting refuge against the risks of refusing it — and it is the Director-General of Shipping and the maritime administration who coordinate it on the Indian side.

Directions to the master, owner or salvor. Under Part XA the Central Government and the Director-General may direct the ship to move, to take or refrain from specified action, or to be salved — and this is the power that turns a commercial decision into a compellable one.
Navigational safety. Marking the casualty, a navigational warning, and where necessary an exclusion or safety zone around it.

blocks.h: 5. Steps for the marine environment

blocks.p: This is the second half of the stem's own question and it has its own actors.

ol: The ship acts first — the SOPEP is implemented, the source is stopped, and containment is attempted with the ship's own means.

The national response is mounted under the National Oil Spill Disaster Contingency Plan, for which the Indian Coast Guard is responsible at sea in India's maritime zones. The plan is tiered, escalating from a local response with local resources to a national and, where necessary, international mobilisation of equipment and expertise.

Response operations — aerial and satellite surveillance to establish the extent and drift of the slick, containment with booms, mechanical recovery with skimmers, dispersant application where and only where it is authorised for those waters and that oil, protection of sensitive shorelines and intakes, shoreline clean-up, and waste reception and disposal.

The statutory directions power is the legal engine of all of it. Under Part XA of the Act — the prevention and containment of pollution of the sea by oil, at sections 356J, 356K and 356L — the Central Government and the Director-General of Shipping may give directions to the owner, the master or the salvor for the prevention or containment of pollution, may take the action themselves where the directions are not complied with or where the case requires it, and may recover the cost from the owner. That is the answer to the stem's 'who should initiate': for the environment, the initiator is the Central Government acting through the Director-General of Shipping, with the Indian Coast Guard executing the response at sea.
Coordination with the coastal State machinery — State pollution control boards, fisheries and environment departments, and port authorities where the shoreline or a port is affected.

Funding. The response is funded through the owner's P&I cover and the compulsory insurance behind the CLC or Bunkers certificate, with the certificate supporting direct action against the insurer — which is why the certificates in Q6 on this paper matter operationally and not only on paper.

blocks.h: 6. Investigation and inquiry - two systems, and both are engaged

blocks.p: This is where most candidates lose marks, because there are two parallel systems with different purposes and they must not be merged.
The national system, under the Merchant Shipping Act, 1958. The Act's Part on investigations and inquiries into shipping casualties provides the machinery, and it runs in stages:

ol: A report of the casualty to the Administration.
A preliminary inquiry, conducted by a person appointed for the purpose, to establish the facts and to advise whether more is required.
Where the circumstances warrant it, a formal investigation before a court sitting with assessors of nautical or engineering experience.

The formal investigation may make findings of fault and may cancel or suspend the certificate of a master, mate or engineer whose conduct caused or contributed to the casualty. Its orientation is therefore partly disciplinary.

blocks.p: The international system, under the Casualty Investigation Code, resolution MSC.255(84), made mandatory by SOLAS regulation XI-1/6. Its purpose is expressly not to apportion blame or liability but to prevent recurrence by establishing causal factors.

And it is mandatory here. A marine safety investigation under the Code is required for a very serious marine casualty — one involving the total loss of the ship, a death, or severe damage to the environment. This casualty is stated to involve loss of lives, so the mandatory limb is engaged, and it would be engaged by the pollution limb only if the environmental damage were severe. The flag State — India, for this vessel — is the marine safety investigating State, and where the other vessel is foreign flagged her flag State and any State whose environment or interests are seriously harmed is a substantially interested State entitled to participate. The report is submitted to the IMO.

Hold the two apart in one sentence: the national inquiry can take a certificate away; the safety investigation exists so that the same accident does not happen twice, and its findings are not to be used to apportion blame.

blocks.h: 7. Liability, compensation and the certificates behind them

blocks.p: The final group of steps is the one that pays for everything in sections 4 and 5, and it should be stated briefly rather than omitted.

ul: Pollution liability. Where she is a CLC ship carrying persistent oil, CLC 1992 imposes strict liability on the owner of the ship for pollution damage, with limitation and compulsory insurance; where she is not, the 2001 Bunkers Convention covers pollution from bunker oil. Whether CLC applies turns on two facts — is she a CLC ship, and is the oil persistent — and it must not be stated absolutely.

Collision liability between the two ships, apportioned according to fault, and pursued in the appropriate forum — in India, the admiralty jurisdiction of the High Courts under the Admiralty (Jurisdiction and Settlement of Maritime Claims) Act, 2017.
Loss of life claims, and the owner's obligations to the crew and their dependants.
Limitation of liability for maritime claims, invoked by the owner in the appropriate forum.
Wreck removal, if the casualty leaves a wreck, under the Act's wreck and salvage Part and its rules.

blocks.p: The one-sentence answer to the stem's 'who'. The Master initiates everything in the first hour; the owner and company initiate the commercial and technical response through the safety management system; the Director-General of Shipping, for the Central Government, initiates and compels the statutory response and holds the inquiry; the Indian Coast Guard executes the pollution response at sea; and the coastal State decides on a place of refuge. Every one of those is an answer to the question, and an answer naming only one of them is incomplete.

blocks.h: Why this structure scores

blocks.p: The stem is a scenario with two express demands — what steps, and who initiates them — and a two-part object: the safety of the ships and the marine environment. Sections 4 and 5 answer those two objects directly, in the stem's own order, and every section names its actor. An answer that describes procedures without saying who owns each one has answered half the question however good the procedures are.

Section 1 exists because the casualty is four events at once, and separating them is what lets the rest of the answer be organised rather than narrated. Section 6 exists because the investigation limb is where marks are most often lost, and because the loss of life in this scenario changes the answer.

blocks.h: The fact in the scenario that changes the law

blocks.p: 'Resulting in the loss of lives.' Under the Casualty Investigation Code a marine safety investigation is mandatory for a very serious marine casualty — total loss of the ship, a death, or severe damage to the environment. A casualty short of that falls under recommended practice.

So in this scenario the mandatory limb is engaged, and it is engaged by the death, not automatically by the oil spill. A spill engages it only if the environmental damage is severe. Getting that reasoning the right way round is the single most examinable point in the question, and it is the reason the printed word 'lives' is in the stem at all.

blocks.h: The statute boundary — and why it is the first thing to get right

blocks.p: The Merchant Shipping Act, 1958 governs this sitting. The Merchant Shipping Act, 2025 received assent on 18 August 2025 and commenced on 15 March 2026 — five months and twelve and a half months after this paper respectively. Nothing from it may appear in this answer.

This is not a theoretical risk. A fully solved question elsewhere in this corpus is built on the 2025 Act, has the same statute title, and is the superficially obvious donor for any Indian merchant shipping question. It was examined and rejected outright for the February 2024 sitting, and it is rejected here for the same reason.

blocks.h: Common mistakes

ul: Citing the Merchant Shipping Act, 2025. It commenced on 15 March 2026, over a year after this sitting.
Writing a narrative of the casualty instead of answering 'what steps' and 'who initiates'.
Naming only the Master. The question's 'who' has at least six answers.
Merging the MS Act inquiry with the Casualty Investigation Code investigation.
Saying a Code investigation is mandatory because there was a spill. It is mandatory here because there was a death; a spill engages it only if the environmental damage is severe.
Omitting the Part XA directions power, which is the legal engine of the whole environmental response and the direct answer to 'who should initiate'.
Forgetting preservation of evidence — VDR, logs, charts, printouts — which decides both the investigation and the liability.
Citing the superseded places of refuge resolution. The current edition is A.1184(33), adopted 6 December 2023.
Stating that CLC applies absolutely. It turns on whether she is a CLC ship and whether the oil is persistent.
Inventing section numbers of the 1958 Act. Name the Part; give a section only where you are sure.

blocks.h: Examiner traps

ul: 'Loss of lives' is not scenery. It is the fact that makes the safety investigation mandatory.
'Who should initiate such steps' is half the question and is the half most often left out. Name an actor for every step.
'For the safety of the ships and the marine environment' is a two-part object printed in the stem. Give each its own section, in that order.
'The Merchant Shipping Act' is printed without a year. At this sitting it can only be the 1958 Act, and saying so explicitly costs one line and protects the whole answer.
The stem says 'ships', plural. A second vessel is involved throughout — her master's duties, her flag State's interest in the investigation, and the apportionment of collision liability.

This is an Engineering Management paper. The Chief Engineer's own contribution — stopping the source, internal transfer, damage and stability assessment, machinery records — is properly part of the answer.

blocks.h: Uncertainty and jurisdiction notes

blocks.p: The corpus does not hold the Merchant Shipping Act, 1958. It holds the 2025 Act — the exact inverse of what this sitting requires — and that is recorded as an accepted limitation rather than worked around by citing the wrong statute.

The section-number discipline is therefore conservative and explicit. The only section numbers asserted are the three groups already established in this corpus for this same machinery — ss.356J, 356K and 356L, ss.390 to 404 and ss.334 to 336 — each carried as authoritative secondary and flagged. The investigations and inquiries Part and the collisions Part, both of which carry substantial weight in this answer, are named at Part level only and no section number is asserted for either. Inventing a section number is the specific failure this discipline exists to prevent.

The National Oil Spill Disaster Contingency Plan is not held: its existence, custodian and tiered structure are stated and no provision, revision or tier threshold is asserted. No DG Shipping circular is cited, the corpus holding none.

The printed scenario does not say whether the other vessel is Indian or foreign flagged. Both are addressed, because a foreign flag makes her flag State a substantially interested State in the safety investigation.

No provision, section number or scheme of the 2025 Act appears anywhere in this object. known_traps.md section 11 applied.

THE MOST DANGEROUS DONOR IN THE CORPUS FOR THIS SUBJECT WAS REJECTED, AS IT WAS FOR FEBRUARY 2024. QP2607-Q7 is a fully solved question on the Merchant Shipping Act 2025 - the same statute title and the superficially obvious donor for any Indian merchant shipping question. QP2402-Q8's temporal record documents rejecting it outright; the same rejection is made here and for the same reason.
THE COASTAL SHIPPING ACT, 2025 IS LIKEWISE POST-SITTING and is excluded.

THE PLACES OF REFUGE EDITION WAS CHECKED AGAINST THIS SITTING. Resolution A.1184(33) was adopted 6 DECEMBER 2023 by the 33rd Assembly and revokes A.949(23). It is fifteen months old at this sitting and is the operative edition. THE CASUALTY INVESTIGATION CODE THRESHOLD WAS APPLIED IN THE CANDIDATE'S FAVOUR AND FOR THE RIGHT REASON. known_traps.md section 5 warns that the Code is NOT engaged by every pollution incident and that a mandatory investigation is required only for a VERY SERIOUS MARINE CASUALTY. Here the printed scenario states LOSS OF LIVES, so the mandatory limb IS engaged - by the death, not by the spill. The answer says so expressly and states that a spill alone would engage it only if the environmental damage were severe.

A LATER CANDIDATE WAS REJECTED ON DIRECTION OF TRAVEL. QP2512-Q5 (December 2025, Indian inquiries into casualties on FOREIGN ships) was the second-strongest match and was not read into this answer, on direction and on scope.

The hidden demand is the statute boundary: the stem prints 'the Merchant Shipping Act' with no year, and at this sitting it can only be the 1958 Act. The scenario detail that changes the law is the loss of lives, which makes a marine safety investigation mandatory.

Sections 2 and 3 carry the immediate and reporting steps, section 6 the investigation limb where marks are most often lost, and section 7 the liability layer briefly. Seven sections give every actor and every object a home.
decomposition_gate.examiner_expectation: The 1958 Act identified as the governing statute. questions.understand_first: Read the scenario as four legal events happening at once, because each starts a different machine and the question asks who as well as what. There is a collision, which engages both masters' duties and the apportionment of fault. There is loss of life — and that word is not scenery: it makes this a very serious marine casualty, so a marine safety investigation under the Casualty Investigation Code becomes mandatory, which it would not be for the spill alone unless the environmental damage were severe. There is damage, which engages seaworthiness, survey, detention and possibly salvage. And there is an oil spill, which engages the national response and the liability conventions. The statute is the Merchant Shipping Act, 1958 — the 2025 Act did not commence until 15 March 2026, more than a year after this sitting. And notice what kind of statute it is: mostly it does not tell the shipowner what to do, it gives the Central Government and the Director-General of Shipping power to direct him, to act themselves if he does not, and to recover the cost. That is the answer to 'who should initiate' for the environmental half, and it is the sentence the whole answer is built around.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Which Merchant Shipping Act applies to a March 2025 casualty?
retrieval_cards.answer: The Merchant Shipping Act, 1958. The Merchant Shipping Act, 2025 received assent on 18 August 2025 and commenced on 15 March 2026 — five and twelve and a half months after this sitting respectively. No provision or section number of the 2025 Act may appear in the answer.
retrieval_cards.why: The stem prints 'the Merchant Shipping Act' with no year, and the wrong statute poisons every citation in the answer.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Is a marine safety investigation mandatory here, and why?
retrieval_cards.answer: Yes — because of the loss of life. Under the Casualty Investigation Code (MSC.255(84), mandatory via SOLAS XI-1/6) an investigation is mandatory for a very serious marine casualty, which includes one involving the total loss of the ship, a death, or severe damage to the environment. The oil spill alone would engage the mandatory limb only if the environmental damage were severe; lesser casualties fall under recommended practice.
retrieval_cards.why: The reasoning must run through the death, not the spill. This is the most examinable point in the question and the reason 'lives' is in the printed stem.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Which provision is the legal engine of the environmental response, and who exercises it?
retrieval_cards.answer: Part XA of the Merchant Shipping Act, 1958 — sections 356J, 356K and 356L. The Central Government and the Director-General of Shipping may give directions to the owner, master or salvor for the prevention or containment of pollution, may take the action themselves where those directions are not complied with, and may recover the cost from the owner. The Indian Coast Guard executes the response at sea.
retrieval_cards.why: It is the direct answer to the stem's 'who should initiate such steps ... for the marine environment'.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Distinguish the MS Act inquiry from the Casualty Investigation Code investigation.
retrieval_cards.answer: MS Act inquiry — report, then a preliminary inquiry by an appointed person, then where warranted a formal investigation before a court with assessors, which may find fault and may cancel or suspend a certificate. Partly disciplinary. Code investigation — a marine safety investigation whose purpose is to establish causal factors and prevent recurrence, and which is expressly not to be used to apportion blame or liability. The report goes to the IMO.
retrieval_cards.why: Merging the two is the classic error, and their purposes are not merely different but opposed.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Give the Master's immediate steps in the right order.
retrieval_cards.answer: Life, ship, environment, evidence. Muster, account for all persons and search for the missing; render assistance to the other vessel and to persons in danger so far as possible without serious danger to his own ship, stand by and exchange particulars; sound tanks, assess damage, stability and residual strength; stop the source and deploy the SOPEP; broadcast and report; and preserve evidence — VDR, charts, logs, engine and alarm records.
retrieval_cards.why: The order is examinable, and preservation of evidence is the step most often omitted, though it decides both the investigation and the liability.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Who decides on a place of refuge, and under what guidance?
retrieval_cards.answer: The coastal State decides, on an objective analysis of the risks of granting refuge against the risks of refusing it. The current guidance is resolution A.1184(33), Guidelines on places of refuge for ships in need of assistance, adopted by the 33rd Assembly on 6 December 2023, revoking A.949(23). On the Indian side the Director-General of Shipping and the maritime administration coordinate it.
retrieval_cards.why: The edition matters, and the answer to 'who decides' is the coastal State - not the owner, the salvor or the flag State.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Who can stop the ship from proceeding, and under what power?
retrieval_cards.answer: The Director-General of Shipping, or a surveyor acting for him, under the unseaworthy and unsafe ships provisions of the 1958 Act at sections 334 to 336, which empower detention of a ship unsafe by reason of defective hull or machinery, undermanning, overloading or improper loading. A damaged ship after a collision is squarely within that power. Separately, Part XA directions can compel her to move or to refrain from moving.
retrieval_cards.why: The stem asks about the safety of the ships, and the compelling power - not the survey - is what answers it.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Answer the stem's 'who' in one sentence.
retrieval_cards.answer: The Master initiates everything in the first hour; the owner and company initiate the technical and commercial response through the safety management system; the Director-General of Shipping, for the Central Government, directs and compels the statutory response and holds the inquiry; the Indian Coast Guard executes the pollution response at sea; and the coastal State decides on a place of refuge.
retrieval_cards.why: Half the question is 'who', and an answer naming only the Master is incomplete however good the procedures are.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Does CLC 1992 cover this spill?
retrieval_cards.answer: It depends, and it must not be stated absolutely. CLC covers persistent hydrocarbon mineral oil carried as cargo or in the bunkers of such a ship. So it turns on two facts: is she a CLC ship, and is the oil persistent? If she is not a CLC ship, the 2001 Bunkers Convention covers bunker pollution. Either way the compulsory insurance certificate supports direct action against the insurer, which is how the response gets funded.
retrieval_cards.why: A standing correction in this corpus, and it links the casualty to the certificates in Q6 on the same paper.
